rd-school-c8-science-a.ch03-coal-petrole.title: Coal and Petroleum — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch03-coal-petrole.subtitle: Inexhaustible vs exhaustible, coal and its products, petroleum refining, natural gas, and saving fuels

sections.md:
Everything we use comes from nature, directly or after processing. Natural resources are of two kinds:

| Inexhaustible | Exhaustible |
|---|---|
| Present in unlimited quantity; not likely to be used up by human activity | Limited in nature; can be used up |
| Sunlight, air | Forests, minerals, coal, petroleum, natural gas |

Some resources, like forests and wildlife, are exhaustible but can be renewed if we use them wisely; coal and petroleum took millions of years to form and **cannot be renewed in a human lifetime**.

Coal, petroleum and natural gas are **fossil fuels** — formed from the dead remains of living organisms (fossils).

**Activity idea:** list things in your house that come from coal or petroleum — the cooking gas, the bus fuel, plastic buckets, polyester clothes, road tar. The list is surprisingly long.

check.q: Which of these is an inexhaustible natural resource?
check.why: Sunlight is available in unlimited amounts and is not used up by human activity.

sections.md:
Coal is hard and black, and is mainly **carbon**. About **300 million years ago** the earth had dense forests in low-lying wetlands. Floods buried these forests under soil; more and more soil piled on top. Deep inside, under **high pressure and high temperature** and without air, the plant matter slowly turned into coal. This slow change of dead vegetation into coal is called **carbonisation**. Because it formed from remains of vegetation, coal is a fossil fuel.

**Uses.** Coal was used for cooking and to run railway engines; it is still used in **thermal power plants** to make electricity and in some industries. Burning coal produces mainly **carbon dioxide**.

**Products of processing coal (heating in industry):**

- **Coke** — tough, porous, black; almost pure carbon. Used to make **steel** and to extract many metals.
- **Coal tar** — thick, black, bad-smelling liquid, a mixture of about **200 substances**. Products from it are used to make synthetic dyes, drugs, explosives, perfumes, plastics, paints, photographic materials and roofing materials. **Naphthalene balls** that repel moths come from coal tar. Coal tar was used for metalling roads; today **bitumen**, a petroleum product, is used instead.
- **Coal gas** — obtained while making coke. Used as fuel in many industries near coal plants. It was first used for street lighting in **London in 1810** and in **New York around 1820**; today it is used as a heat source rather than for lighting.

Petrol and diesel come from **petroleum**. It formed from organisms living in the **sea**. When they died, their bodies settled at the sea bed and were covered with layers of sand and clay. Over millions of years, absence of air, high temperature and high pressure changed them into **petroleum and natural gas**.

The oil and gas lie in porous rock layers trapped between non-porous layers; gas sits above the oil and water below. The world's first oil well was drilled in **Pennsylvania, USA, in 1859**. Eight years later, in **1867**, oil was struck at **Makum in Assam**. In India oil is found in Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai High, and the river basins of Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.

**Refining.** Petroleum is a dark oily liquid with an unpleasant smell, a mixture of many components. Separating them is called **refining**, done in a **petroleum refinery**.

| Constituent | Use |
|---|---|
| Petroleum gas (LPG) | Fuel for homes and industry |
| Petrol | Motor fuel, aviation fuel, solvent for dry cleaning |
| Kerosene | Fuel for stoves, lamps, jet aircraft |
| Diesel | Heavy motor vehicles, electric generators |
| Lubricating oil | Lubrication |
| Paraffin wax | Ointments, candles, Vaseline |
| Bitumen | Paints, road surfacing |

Many useful substances from petroleum and natural gas are **petrochemicals** — used in detergents, polyester, nylon, acrylic, polythene and fertilisers (urea; hydrogen from natural gas). Because of its great commercial importance, petroleum is called **black gold**.

check.q: Which petroleum product is used for surfacing roads?
check.why: Bitumen is the heavy residue from refining and is used for road surfacing and paints.

sections.md:
Natural gas is a very important fossil fuel because it is easy to transport through **pipes**. It is stored under high pressure as **compressed natural gas (CNG)** and used for power generation, and as fuel for buses, autos and cars — CNG is a **cleaner fuel** than petrol and diesel, which is why Delhi's buses and autos switched to it.

In India natural gas is found in **Tripura, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, and the Krishna–Godavari delta**. It is piped to homes and factories in many cities. It is also a starting material for many chemicals and fertilisers.

> **Note from the chapter:** coal, petroleum and natural gas cannot be prepared from dead organisms in a laboratory — their formation needs millions of years.

check.q: Why is CNG called a cleaner fuel?
options: It produces less pollution when burnt than petrol or diesel
check.why: Burning CNG gives far fewer pollutants than petrol and diesel, so it pollutes the air less.

sections.h: Some natural resources are limited — save fuel!
sections.md:
Fossil fuels are limited and their burning pollutes air and is linked to **global warming**. The **Petroleum Conservation Research Association (PCRA)** in India advises drivers how to save fuel:

- Drive at a constant and moderate speed as far as possible.
- Switch off the engine at traffic lights or while waiting.
- Keep tyre pressure correct.
- Ensure regular maintenance of the vehicle.

Other ways: use public transport, cycle or walk for short distances, car-pool, and switch to cleaner and renewable sources like solar and wind where possible.

> **Did you know?** Known reserves of coal and petroleum will last only some hundreds of years at the present rate of use — a blink in the millions of years they took to form.

check.q: Which practice saves fuel while driving?
options: Switching off the engine at long red lights
check.why: Switching off at traffic lights stops fuel being burnt while the vehicle is not moving.

summary: Inexhaustible resources (sunlight, air) are unlimited; exhaustible ones (coal, petroleum, forests, minerals) are limited.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels made from dead organisms over millions of years.
Carbonisation is the slow conversion of dead vegetation into coal under heat and pressure without air.
Coal gives coke, coal tar and coal gas; coke is used for steel.
Coal tar gives dyes, drugs, explosives, paints, plastics and naphthalene balls.
Petroleum formed from marine organisms; India's first oil was struck at Makum, Assam, in 1867.
Refining separates LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and bitumen.
Petrochemicals give detergents, fibres, polythene and fertilisers; petroleum is called black gold.
Natural gas is piped and stored as CNG, a cleaner fuel.
PCRA tips: steady moderate speed, engine off at lights, correct tyre pressure, regular servicing.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch04-combustion-f.title: Combustion and Flame
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch04-combustion-f.subtitle: Why a matchstick bursts into fire, why water fights it, and what the colours of a candle flame mean

sections.md:
On Diwali night, a whole street glows with diyas. A tiny cotton wick, a little oil, a single flame — and yet some diyas flicker out in the wind while others burn till dawn. Why does the oil burn but the clay lamp does not? Why does a flame have colours? Why do firefighters use water on a burning house but foam on a burning petrol tanker?

All these questions are about **combustion**.

**Combustion** is a chemical process in which a substance **reacts with oxygen** to give off **heat**. The substance that undergoes combustion is called **combustible** or a **fuel**. The fuel may be solid (coal, wood), liquid (petrol, kerosene) or gas (LPG, CNG). Sometimes **light** is also given off, either as a flame or as a glow.

When magnesium ribbon burns, it gives a dazzling white light and forms magnesium oxide. Charcoal burns in air to produce carbon dioxide, heat and light.

Substances such as **stone, glass, iron nails** do not catch fire — they are **non-combustible**.

Our body, too, 'burns' food slowly: food breaks down with oxygen to release energy. That is a slow form of combustion inside cells — respiration.

check.q: Which of these is non-combustible?
check.why: Glass does not react with oxygen to give heat, so it does not burn.

sections.md:
Try this safely with a teacher: light a candle and cover it with an inverted glass tumbler. The flame flickers and dies within seconds. Why? It used up the **oxygen (air)** inside.

Now think of a matchstick: rub it on the box and it lights. Hold an unlit matchstick near a flame and it lights only once it gets hot enough.

Fire needs three things together — the **fire triangle**:
1. **Fuel** — something combustible.
2. **Air (oxygen)** — to support combustion.
3. **Heat** — enough to raise the fuel to its **ignition temperature**.

**Ignition temperature** is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. A substance cannot catch fire or burn as long as its temperature is below its ignition temperature.

Try heating water in a paper cup over a candle. The cup does not burn! The heat passes to the water, so the paper never reaches its ignition temperature.

**Inflammable substances** have very low ignition temperatures and catch fire easily: petrol, alcohol, LPG. Keep them far from flames.

Kerosene oil and wood do not catch fire on their own at room temperature. Heat kerosene a little and it catches fire. Wood needs more heating — its ignition temperature is higher.

check.q: Water in a paper cup can be boiled over a flame without the cup burning because…
options: Water absorbs the heat so paper stays below its ignition temperature
There is no oxygen near the cup
check.why: Heat passes into the water, so the paper never reaches the temperature at which it would catch fire.

sections.md:
Matches have a long history. About five thousand years ago, small pieces of pinewood dipped in sulphur were used as matches in ancient Egypt. Later, the head of a match carried antimony trisulphide and potassium chlorate, and was rubbed on rough sandpaper mixed with powdered glass. But white phosphorus used in early matches was dangerous for workers and users.

In a **safety match** today:
- The **head** has antimony trisulphide and potassium chlorate.
- The **rubbing surface** on the box has **powdered glass and a little red phosphorus**.

When you strike the match, the friction makes some red phosphorus turn into white phosphorus, which reacts with potassium chlorate in the head. Enough heat is produced to ignite antimony trisulphide, and combustion starts. That is why a safety match will not light on just any surface.

When a fire breaks out, the fire brigade arrives and sprays water. Water **cools** the combustible material below its ignition temperature and the water vapour also surrounds the fuel, cutting off air. Removing any side of the fire triangle stops the fire.

But water is **not** suitable for every fire:
- **Electrical fires** — water conducts electricity and can electrocute the person fighting the fire.
- **Oil and petrol fires** — water is heavier than oil; it sinks below, and the oil keeps burning on top and spreads.

For these, **carbon dioxide (CO₂)** is the best extinguisher. Being heavier than oxygen, CO₂ covers the fire like a blanket, cutting off oxygen. It also cools the fuel. A big bonus: it usually does not harm electrical equipment. CO₂ is stored at high pressure as a liquid in cylinders. Chemicals like **sodium bicarbonate (baking soda)** or **potassium bicarbonate** release CO₂ near the fire.

At home: if a pan of oil catches fire, **turn off the gas and cover the pan with a lid** — never throw water. If clothes catch fire, **stop, drop and roll**, or wrap in a thick blanket.

right.title: Use CO₂ / sand for…
points: Oil and petrol fires (oil floats on water)
CO₂ blankets the fire and cuts oxygen

check.q: Why is water not used on a petrol fire?
options: Petrol is lighter, floats on water and keeps burning
check.why: Petrol floats on top of water, so the water sinks beneath and the burning layer spreads instead of being smothered.

sections.md:
**Rapid combustion:** bring a burning match near a gas stove with the knob open and the gas burns at once, producing heat and light. Gas burns rapidly.

**Spontaneous combustion:** some substances like **phosphorus** burn in air at room temperature. A material bursting into flames without any apparent cause is spontaneous combustion. Spontaneous combustion of **coal dust** has caused many disasters in coal mines. Forest fires are sometimes caused by the heat of the sun or lightning, which sets off spontaneous combustion of dry leaves — though most forest fires are due to human carelessness.

**Explosion:** when a cracker is ignited, a sudden reaction takes place with the evolution of heat, light and sound. A large amount of gas is formed and liberated. Explosions can also happen if pressure is applied on a cracker.

check.q: Burning of LPG on a stove is an example of…
check.why: LPG catches fire quickly when lit and burns fast with heat and light, which is rapid combustion.

sections.md:
Observe an LPG flame, a kerosene stove, a candle, magnesium ribbon and charcoal. LPG, kerosene and wax burn with a **flame**; charcoal and coal just **glow** red. Why? Substances that **vaporise** during burning give flames. Kerosene oil and molten wax rise through the wick and are vaporised; the vapours burn. Charcoal does not vaporise, so it glows without a flame.

**Structure of a candle flame** (from inside out):

| Zone | Colour | Combustion | Temperature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Innermost | Dark | No combustion — unburnt wax vapour | Least hot |
| Middle | Yellow, luminous | Partial (incomplete) combustion | Moderately hot |
| Outermost | Blue, non-luminous | Complete combustion | **Hottest** |

Goldsmiths blow air through a metal pipe at the **outermost zone** of a flame to melt gold and silver — because it is the hottest part.

**Try it (with a teacher):** hold a glass plate in the luminous zone for 10 seconds. A black ring of soot (unburnt carbon) forms. Hold a glass tube in the dark zone and you can light the wax vapour at the other end!

sections.h: What makes a good fuel? Calorific value
sections.md:
Many fuels exist — cow dung cakes, wood, coal, kerosene, petrol, LPG, CNG, biogas. A **good fuel** is one that:
- is readily available and cheap,
- burns easily in air at a moderate rate,
- produces a large amount of heat,
- does not leave behind any undesirable substances.

No fuel is ideal in every way, so we choose the best for each use.

**Calorific value** is the amount of heat energy produced on complete combustion of **1 kg** of a fuel. It is expressed in **kilojoule per kg (kJ/kg)**.

head: Fuel
Calorific value (kJ/kg)
fig.caption: Approximate calorific values. Hydrogen has the highest, but is hard to store safely.

check.q: Which fuel in the table has the highest calorific value?
check.why: Hydrogen releases about 150000 kJ per kg on complete combustion, far more than any other fuel listed.

sections.md:
Burning fuels causes harm when not done carefully:

- **Unburnt carbon particles** from wood, coal and petroleum are fine particles that pollute air and cause respiratory diseases such as **asthma**.
- **Incomplete combustion** produces **carbon monoxide** — a very poisonous gas. Never sleep in a closed room with a coal fire (angithi) burning: carbon monoxide can kill people while they sleep.
- Combustion of most fuels releases **carbon dioxide**. Increased CO₂ is believed to cause **global warming** — the rise in the temperature of Earth's atmosphere. This can melt polar glaciers, raise sea levels, and flood coastal areas; low-lying islands could be submerged.
- Coal and diesel release **sulphur dioxide**; petrol engines give off oxides of **nitrogen**. These dissolve in rainwater to form acids — **acid rain**, which harms crops, buildings (even the marble of the Taj Mahal) and soil.

That is why vehicles are shifting to **CNG**, which produces harmful products in very small amounts.

check.q: Why is it dangerous to sleep in a closed room with a burning coal angithi?
options: Incomplete combustion produces poisonous carbon monoxide
check.why: In limited air, coal burns incompletely and gives carbon monoxide, an odourless gas that can be fatal.

workedExamples.q: 4.5 kg of a fuel produces 180,000 kJ of heat on complete combustion. Find its calorific value.
How much heat does 2 kg of LPG give (55000 kJ/kg)? How much wood (20000 kJ/kg) gives the same heat?
workedExamples.answer: 110,000 kJ; it would take 5.5 kg of wood.

summary: Combustion is a chemical reaction with oxygen that gives heat, and often light.
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat (to reach ignition temperature).
Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire; inflammable substances have low ignition temperatures.
Safety match: head has antimony trisulphide and potassium chlorate; box surface has powdered glass and red phosphorus.
Water cools and smothers ordinary fires but must not be used on electrical or oil fires; CO₂ is best for those.
Types: rapid combustion, spontaneous combustion, explosion.
Substances that vaporise burn with a flame; charcoal only glows.
Candle flame zones: dark (no combustion), yellow (partial), blue (complete, hottest).
Calorific value = heat from complete combustion of 1 kg fuel, in kJ/kg.
Burning fuels causes particulate pollution, carbon monoxide, global warming and acid rain.

glossary.d: Substance burnt to produce heat
Heat energy from 1 kg of fuel burnt completely
Rise in average temperature of Earth's atmosphere
Rain made acidic by oxides of sulphur and nitrogen
Catching fire with no apparent cause

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch04-combustion-f.title: Combustion and Flame — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch04-combustion-f.subtitle: Conditions for burning, ignition temperature, fire control, types of combustion, the candle flame, fuels and calorific value

sections.h: What is combustion? Combustible and non-combustible
sections.md:
A chemical process in which a substance reacts with **oxygen** to give off **heat** (and often light) is **combustion**. The substance that burns is a **fuel** or **combustible substance**.

**Activity (as in the chapter):** hold straw, matchsticks, kerosene, paper, iron nails, stone pieces and glass with tongs over a flame. Straw, paper, kerosene and matchsticks burn — **combustible**. Iron nails, stone and glass do not — **non-combustible**.

Magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white light, forming magnesium oxide and giving heat — combustion. Charcoal burns in air giving CO₂, heat and light. The sun's heat and light also come from nuclear reactions, not ordinary combustion.

**Air is necessary.** Cover a burning candle with a glass chimney: with the chimney raised on wooden blocks, air enters and the candle burns well; with the chimney sitting on the table and its top covered by a glass plate, the flame flickers and dies — no fresh oxygen.

A matchstick doesn't burn on its own at room temperature; you must strike it. The **lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire** is its **ignition temperature**.

**Paper-cup activity:** heat water in a paper cup over a candle. The cup does not burn because the heat goes into the water, keeping the paper below its ignition temperature. Kerosene catches fire easily but wood needs more heating — kerosene has a lower ignition temperature.

Substances with **very low ignition temperatures** that catch fire easily with a flame are **inflammable**: petrol, alcohol, LPG. Handle them carefully.

**The matchstick story.** Over 5,000 years ago in ancient Egypt, small pieces of pinewood dipped in sulphur were used as matches. Modern safety matches carry a mixture of **antimony trisulphide and potassium chlorate** on the head, while the rubbing surface has **powdered glass and a little red phosphorus**. Striking turns some red phosphorus into white phosphorus, which reacts with potassium chlorate, producing enough heat to ignite the head. Earlier white phosphorus matches were dangerous for workers and users.

check.q: Why doesn't the paper cup with water burn over a candle?
options: Water absorbs the heat, so the paper stays below its ignition temperature
check.why: Heat flows into the water, so the paper never reaches its ignition temperature.

sections.md:
Three things are needed for fire: **fuel, air (oxygen) and heat** to raise the fuel to its ignition temperature. Fire is controlled by removing one or more of these.

- **Water** is the commonest extinguisher: it cools the combustible material below its ignition temperature, and its vapour surrounds the material, cutting off air.
- **Water must not be used for electrical fires** (it conducts electricity and can harm those using it) or for **oil and petrol fires** (water is heavier, sinks below the oil, and the oil keeps burning on top).
- **Carbon dioxide (CO₂)** is the best extinguisher for electrical and oil fires. Being heavier than oxygen, it covers the fire like a blanket, cutting off oxygen, and also cools the fuel. It is stored as liquid under pressure in cylinders; sodium/potassium bicarbonate powder near the fire also releases CO₂.
- Switch off the electric main first. If clothes catch fire, wrap the person in a blanket and roll on the ground.

Fire brigades keep large reserves of water and CO₂ extinguishers.

check.q: Why should water not be used on a petrol fire?
options: Water sinks below petrol, which keeps burning on top
check.why: Water is heavier than oil and petrol, so it sinks beneath them and the burning fuel spreads on top.

sections.md:
- **Rapid combustion:** a gas burns quickly producing heat and light — bring a burning match near a gas stove.
- **Spontaneous combustion:** a substance suddenly bursts into flames without any apparent cause. Example: white phosphorus burns in air at room temperature. Spontaneous combustion of coal dust has caused disasters in coal mines, and some **forest fires** start this way in hot weather (though most are caused by human carelessness).
- **Explosion:** a sudden reaction with heat, light and sound, releasing a large amount of gas — **fire-crackers** when ignited; explosions can also happen when pressure is applied to a cracker.

check.q: White phosphorus catching fire in air at room temperature is an example of…
check.why: It bursts into flame on its own without being lit, which is spontaneous combustion.

sections.h: Flame and the structure of a candle flame
sections.md:
LPG, kerosene and wax **vaporise** during burning and form flames; charcoal glows red but gives no flame because it does not vaporise. Wood burns with a flame because its volatile substances vaporise.

A **candle flame** has three zones:

| Zone | Colour | Temperature | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Innermost | Dark | Least hot | Unburnt wax vapour |
| Middle (luminous) | Yellow | Moderately hot | Partial combustion; glowing carbon particles |
| Outermost (non-luminous) | Blue | Hottest | Complete combustion |

**Evidence from activities:** a glass tube held in the dark zone lets wax vapour escape and burn at its other end. A glass plate held in the luminous zone gets a black ring of **unburnt carbon** (soot). Goldsmiths blow through a metal pipe onto the **outermost zone** to melt gold and silver, because it is the hottest.

check.q: Which zone of a candle flame is the hottest?
check.why: Complete combustion happens in the outermost blue zone, making it the hottest.

sections.h: Fuels, calorific value and burning fuels harm the environment
sections.md:
A **good fuel** is readily available, cheap, burns easily in air at a moderate rate, produces a large amount of heat and leaves no undesirable substances. No fuel is ideal; we choose the one that best fits.

The amount of heat produced by complete combustion of **1 kg** of a fuel is its **calorific value**, measured in **kJ/kg**.

| Fuel | Calorific value (kJ/kg) |
|---|---|
| Cow dung cake | 6,000–8,000 |
| Wood | 17,000–22,000 |
| Coal | 25,000–33,000 |
| Petrol | 45,000 |
| Kerosene | 45,000 |
| Diesel | 45,000 |
| Methane | 50,000 |
| CNG | 50,000 |
| LPG | 55,000 |
| Biogas | 35,000–40,000 |
| Hydrogen | 150,000 |

**Harm from burning fuels:**
- Unburnt carbon particles cause respiratory diseases such as asthma.
- Incomplete combustion gives **carbon monoxide**, a very poisonous gas — never sleep in a closed room with a burning coal fire.
- Increased **CO₂** causes **global warming**: polar ice melts, sea levels rise, coastal areas flood.
- Burning coal and diesel releases **sulphur dioxide**; petrol engines release **oxides of nitrogen**. These dissolve in rain to form **acid rain**, harmful to crops, buildings and soil.
- Hence the shift to CNG and cleaner fuels.

check.q: Why is it dangerous to sleep in a closed room with a coal fire burning?
options: Carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion can poison the people
check.why: Limited air causes incomplete combustion, producing carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas that can kill.

How much heat does 2 kg of LPG give (calorific value 55,000 kJ/kg)?

Substances that burn are combustible; iron, stone and glass are non-combustible.

Inflammable substances (petrol, alcohol, LPG) have very low ignition temperatures.
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat; controlling fire removes one of these.
Water cools fires but is unsafe for electrical and oil fires; CO₂ is best for these.
Types: rapid, spontaneous and explosion.
A candle flame has a dark inner, yellow luminous middle and blue hottest outer zone.
Calorific value is heat from 1 kg of fuel in kJ/kg; hydrogen is highest.
Burning fuels cause soot, CO poisoning, global warming and acid rain.

sections.md:
Imagine a village elder pointing at a bare hillside. 'When I was your age,' she says, 'that hill was so thick with sal and teak that we could not see the sky. Leopards came down to drink at the stream. Now — look.' Where did the forest go?

The answer has a name: **deforestation** — clearing forests and using the land for other purposes.

**Causes of deforestation:**
- Procuring land for **cultivation**
- Building **houses and factories**
- Making **furniture** or using wood as **fuel**
- **Natural causes**: forest fires and severe droughts

**Consequences:**
- Rise in temperature and pollution level on Earth
- Increase in the level of **carbon dioxide** in the atmosphere (fewer trees to absorb it), contributing to **global warming**
- **Ground water level lowers**
- Disturbs the balance in nature and the rainfall pattern; fewer rains can lead to **droughts**, while bare soil leads to **floods**
- **Soil erosion**: without roots holding it, the fertile top soil is washed away; soil loses water-holding capacity
- **Desertification**: fertile land gradually turns into a desert

Trees also give us oxygen, food, medicines, and homes for countless animals. Losing them affects everyone.

sections.md:
To protect our flora (plants) and fauna (animals) and their habitats, the government sets aside protected areas: **wildlife sanctuaries, national parks and biosphere reserves**. In these, plantation, cultivation, grazing, felling trees, hunting and poaching are prohibited or restricted.

| Area | What it protects | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Wildlife sanctuary** | Animals and their habitat; some activities like grazing by locals may be allowed | Pachmarhi Wildlife Sanctuary, Bori Sanctuary (MP) |
| **National park** | Large area protecting the whole ecosystem — flora, fauna, landscape, historic objects | Satpura National Park, Jim Corbett, Kaziranga |
| **Biosphere reserve** | Large area conserving biodiversity *and* the culture of local people; contains other protected areas within it | Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve, Nilgiri, Sundarbans |

**Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve** in Madhya Pradesh contains one national park (**Satpura**) and two wildlife sanctuaries (**Bori** and **Pachmarhi**). Satpura is home to India's finest teak. Its rock shelters show prehistoric paintings — evidence of people who lived there thousands of years ago; they show animals and figures fighting, dancing and playing instruments.

**Biodiversity** (biological diversity) means the variety of organisms existing on Earth, their interrelationships and their relationship with the environment.
keyTerms: Flora — plants of an area
Fauna — animals of an area
Biodiversity — variety of life and its interrelations
Biosphere — the part of Earth where living things exist

check.q: Satpura National Park is part of which biosphere reserve?
check.why: Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve in Madhya Pradesh includes Satpura National Park and the Bori and Pachmarhi sanctuaries.

sections.md:
**Endemic species** are plants and animals found exclusively in a particular area. They are not naturally found anywhere else. A particular type of animal or plant may be endemic to a zone, a state or a country.

In Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve: **sal** and **wild mango** are endemic flora; **bison, Indian giant squirrel** and **flying squirrel** are endemic fauna.

Other Indian examples: the **lion-tailed macaque** of the Western Ghats, the **Nilgiri tahr**, and the **Indian rhinoceros** largely in Assam.

Endemic species are especially at risk. If their only habitat is destroyed, they have nowhere else to go. When the growing human population encroaches on their land, or a new species arrives, their natural habitat is disturbed and they may become endangered.

**Species** is a group of population capable of **interbreeding** — members of one species can reproduce fertile offspring only with members of their own species. Members of a species share common characteristics.

check.q: An endemic species is one that…
options: Is found all over the world
Is found only in a particular area
check.why: Endemic species occur naturally only in a specific region and nowhere else.

sections.h: Endangered animals and the story of the tiger
sections.md:
Animals whose numbers are diminishing to a level that they might face **extinction** are known as **endangered animals**. The **dinosaurs** vanished millions of years ago — that is extinction on a grand scale. Today, human activity is pushing many species toward the same fate.

Small animals are in more danger than big ones in one sense: people sometimes kill snakes, frogs, lizards, bats and owls mercilessly, without realising their importance in the ecosystem.

An **ecosystem** is made of all the plants, animals and microorganisms in an area along with non-living components such as climate, soil, river and deltas.

**Project Tiger** was launched by the Government of India on **1 April 1973** to protect tigers. Tiger reserves were created where tigers could live safely. **Satpura Tiger Reserve** is one. Tiger numbers had fallen badly through hunting and habitat loss. In recent surveys India's tiger population has risen and India now has around three-quarters of the world's wild tigers — a real conservation success, though threats remain.

Other endangered animals in India include the **one-horned rhinoceros**, **great Indian bustard**, **snow leopard**, and **Ganges river dolphin**.

items.what: Ministry of Environment and Forests set up
Cheetahs brought from Namibia to Kuno National Park

fig.caption: Milestones in Indian wildlife conservation.

check.q: Project Tiger was launched in…
check.why: The Government of India launched Project Tiger on 1 April 1973 to protect the dwindling tiger population.

sections.md:
The **Red Data Book** is the source book which keeps a record of all the **endangered animals and plants**. It is maintained internationally by an organisation (the IUCN). India also maintains a Red Data Book for its plants and animals.

**Migration** is the phenomenon of movement of a species from its own habitat to some other habitat for a particular time period every year, for a particular purpose like breeding. **Migratory birds** fly to far-away areas every year during a particular time because of climatic changes. They fly long distances to lay eggs as the weather in their natural habitat becomes very cold and inhospitable.

Siberian cranes once came to Bharatpur (Keoladeo National Park, Rajasthan) every winter. Bar-headed geese cross the Himalaya. Flamingos visit the Rann of Kutch and even the creeks of Mumbai.

sections.md:
It takes about **17 full-grown trees to make one tonne of paper**. Paper can be recycled **five to seven times** for use. If each student saves at least one sheet of paper a day, we can save many trees in a year. We should save, reuse used paper and recycle it. This saves trees, energy and water needed to manufacture paper, and reduces harmful chemicals used in paper-making.

**Reforestation** is restocking of the destroyed forests by planting new trees. The planted trees should generally be of the same species as were found in that forest. We should plant at least as many trees as we cut. Reforestation can also take place **naturally** — if a deforested area is left undisturbed, it re-establishes itself.

In India, the **Forest (Conservation) Act** aims at preservation and conservation of natural forests and meeting the basic needs of people living in or near forests.

> Did you know? Jadav Payeng of Majuli, Assam, planted a forest by hand on a sandbar of the Brahmaputra over decades. It is now home to elephants, deer and even tigers — the Molai forest.

check.q: About how many trees are needed for one tonne of paper?
check.why: Roughly 17 full-grown trees are cut to make a tonne of paper, which is why recycling paper saves forests.

sections.md:
Conservation is not only the government's job. Students can:

- Use both sides of paper; carry cloth bags.
- Recycle newspapers and notebooks.
- Plant a tree on your birthday — and care for it until it grows.
- Never buy products made from wild animals (ivory, skins, shells).
- Join or start an eco-club. Organise a cleanliness or plantation drive.
- Learn from the **Chipko movement** of the 1970s in the Garhwal Himalaya, where village women hugged trees to stop them from being felled, and from the Bishnoi community of Rajasthan, known for their long tradition of protecting trees and blackbuck.

Celebrate **Van Mahotsav** in July and **World Environment Day** on 5 June with real action, not just posters.

workedExamples.answer: About 20 trees saved in one year.

sections.md:
In the chapter, Paheli and Boojho visit **Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve** with Prof. Ahmad and wonder what happens when forests vanish.

**Deforestation** means clearing forests and using the land for other purposes.

**Causes:**
- Getting land for cultivation.
- Building houses and factories.
- Making furniture or using wood as fuel.
- Natural causes: **forest fires** and severe **droughts**.

**Consequences:**
- Rising temperature and pollution; more **carbon dioxide** in the air → **global warming**.
- The **water cycle** is disturbed; rainfall decreases, causing **droughts**, and also **floods**.
- **Soil erosion**: fewer trees mean roots no longer hold the soil; the top fertile layer washes away, exposing hard rocky layers with less humus. Gradually fertile land turns into **desert** — **desertification**.
- Water-holding capacity of soil drops; less water seeps into the ground.
- Loss of habitat for animals and plants; reduced biodiversity.

check.q: The conversion of fertile land into desert due to deforestation is called…
check.why: When trees are removed, soil erodes and loses fertility until the land becomes desert-like — desertification.

sections.h: Conservation of forest and wildlife: protected areas
sections.md:
To protect flora and fauna, the government has laws and sets aside protected areas:

| Area | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Wildlife sanctuary** | Area where animals and their habitats are protected from disturbance; killing or capturing animals is prohibited |
| **National park** | Large reserved area for wildlife where they can freely use the habitat and natural resources; protects the whole ecosystem |
| **Biosphere reserve** | Large area meant to conserve biodiversity, along with the traditional ways of life of people living there; may contain parks and sanctuaries |

**Biodiversity** is the variety of organisms in an area, their interrelations and their relation with the environment.

**Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve** (Madhya Pradesh) includes **Satpura National Park** and two wildlife sanctuaries, **Bori and Pachmarhi**. Satpura has India's finest teak; rock shelters there show prehistoric life and paintings.

Even in protected areas, **poaching** (illegal hunting) and cutting threaten wildlife.

Plants of a particular area are its **flora**; animals are its **fauna**.

In Pachmarhi: **flora** — sal, teak, mango, jamun, silver ferns, arjun; **fauna** — chinkara, blue bull (nilgai), barking deer, cheetal, leopard, wild dog, wolf.

**Endemic species** are plants and animals found **exclusively in a particular area** and naturally nowhere else. In Pachmarhi: sal and wild mango (flora); bison, Indian giant squirrel and flying squirrel (fauna).

Endemic species are threatened when their habitat is destroyed, by growing population, or by new species introduced into the area.

sections.h: Wildlife sanctuaries, national parks and Project Tiger
sections.md:
India has many sanctuaries and national parks; Satpura was India's first **reserve forest**.

**Project Tiger** was launched in **1973** to protect tigers and ensure their survival. Satpura is also a tiger reserve. Tigers once roamed widely; hunting and habitat loss made them rare.

**Extinct** animals no longer exist anywhere on Earth (e.g. the dinosaurs; some species vanish because of humans).

**Endangered animals** are those whose numbers have diminished to a level that they might face extinction — e.g. the tiger, the elephant, the wild buffalo and the barasingha.

**Ecosystem:** all the plants, animals and microorganisms of an area along with non-living components like climate, soil, river and deltas. Disturbing one part (say, removing a predator) affects the whole.

check.q: When was Project Tiger launched in India?
check.why: Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect India's tigers and their habitats.

sections.md:
The **Red Data Book** is a source book that keeps a record of all **endangered animals and plants**. It is maintained internationally by an organisation, and India also maintains a Red Data Book for its plants and animals.

**Migration** is the movement of a species from its own habitat to another place for a particular time each year, usually for **breeding**. **Migratory birds** fly long distances to warmer places in winter, when their home becomes cold. For example, birds from colder lands reach Indian wetlands every winter. Some also travel in search of food. (The chapter's Pachmarhi visit had no flamingos, but you can see migratory birds in places like Bharatpur.)

check.q: The Red Data Book records…
check.why: The Red Data Book is the record of species that are endangered and need protection.

sections.h: Recycling paper, reforestation and what you can do
sections.md:
It takes about **17 full-grown trees to make one tonne of paper**. Paper can be **recycled five to seven times** for use. If each student saved at least one sheet a day, we could save many trees a year. We should **save, reuse and recycle** paper — this also saves water and energy, and reduces the harmful chemicals used in paper-making.

**Reforestation** is restocking destroyed forests by planting new trees — preferably the **same species** that grew there. Reforestation can also happen **naturally** if the deforested area is left undisturbed. In India the **Forest (Conservation) Act** aims at the preservation and conservation of natural forests and at meeting the basic needs of people living in or near forests.

**What you can do:** plant and care for trees on Van Mahotsav, use both sides of paper, avoid wasting notebooks, say no to products from endangered animals, and join a nature club.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch06-reproduction.title: Reproduction in Animals
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch06-reproduction.subtitle: How life makes more life — from a dividing amoeba to a frog's tadpoles to a human baby

sections.md:
Every cow, every sparrow, every person alive today exists because an unbroken chain of parents stretches back millions of years. If a species stopped producing young, it would vanish within one lifetime.

**Reproduction** is the production of new individuals of the same kind by their parents. It ensures the **continuation of a species** generation after generation.

In Class 7 you learnt how plants reproduce. Animals too reproduce in two ways:

1. **Sexual reproduction** — involves the fusion of male and female gametes (reproductive cells).
2. **Asexual reproduction** — only a single parent is involved; no gametes fuse.

You may have watched a calf born on a farm, puppies with their mother, or chicks hatching. You may also have seen butterflies laying eggs on leaves. All of these are part of this story.

Like plants, animals have male and female parts. The male produces male gametes; the female produces female gametes.

**Male reproductive organs (humans):** a pair of **testes** (singular: testis), two **sperm ducts** and a **penis**. The testes produce male gametes called **sperms**. Millions of sperms are produced. Each sperm is a **single cell**, tiny, with a **head, a middle piece and a tail**. The tail helps it move.

**Female reproductive organs:** a pair of **ovaries**, **oviducts** (fallopian tubes) and the **uterus**. The ovary produces female gametes called **ova** (eggs). In human beings, a single matured egg is released into the oviduct by one of the ovaries every month. The uterus is where the development of the baby takes place.

Like the sperm, an egg is also a single cell — but much larger. All living things begin life as a single cell, the zygote.

It is natural to feel shy about this topic. Remember: this is the same kind of science as learning how the heart or lungs work, and knowing it helps you understand your own body.
keyTerms: Gamete — reproductive cell (sperm or ovum)
Testis — male organ that produces sperms
Ovary — female organ that produces eggs
Uterus — organ in which the baby develops

check.q: Which part of the sperm helps it to move?
check.why: The tail lashes from side to side, letting the single-celled sperm swim towards the egg.

sections.md:
The first step in sexual reproduction is the fusion of a sperm and an ovum. When they come in contact, the nucleus of the sperm and the nucleus of the egg **fuse** to form a single nucleus. This results in the formation of a **fertilised egg** or **zygote**. The process of fusion is called **fertilisation**.

The zygote receives characteristics from both parents — that is why a child may have the father's eyes and the mother's smile.

**Internal fertilisation:** fertilisation that takes place **inside the female body**. Found in humans, cows, dogs and hens.

**External fertilisation:** fertilisation that takes place **outside the female body**. Very common in aquatic animals such as **fish, starfish and frogs**.

In spring or the rainy season, frogs and toads move to ponds and slow streams. The female lays hundreds of eggs in water. Frog eggs are not covered by a shell; a layer of jelly holds them together and protects them. As the eggs are laid, the male deposits sperms over them. Each sperm swims randomly in water with its long tail and some fuse with eggs.

Why hundreds of eggs? Because they are exposed to water movement, wind and rainfall, and many are eaten by other animals. Many eggs and sperms ensure that at least some are fertilised and survive.

**IVF ('test-tube babies'):** in some cases, doctors fertilise an egg with a sperm outside the body and then implant the early embryo in the mother's uterus to develop normally. The name is misleading — the baby does not grow in a test tube.

left.title: Internal fertilisation
points: Embryo protected inside mother or shelled egg

right.title: External fertilisation
points: Outside the body, usually in water
Eggs exposed to predators and weather

check.q: Why does a frog lay hundreds of eggs?
options: Many eggs are lost to water movement and predators, so more eggs ensure some survive
check.why: With external fertilisation the eggs face many dangers, so laying many raises the chance that some become adult frogs.

sections.md:
Fertilisation results in a zygote, which begins to develop into an **embryo**. The zygote **divides repeatedly** to give rise to a ball of cells. The cells then begin to form groups that develop into different tissues and organs. This developing structure is the embryo.

The embryo gets **embedded in the wall of the uterus** for further development — this is called **implantation**. It continues to develop and gradually forms body parts such as hands, legs, head, eyes and ears. The stage of the embryo in which all body parts can be identified is called a **foetus**. When development is complete, the mother gives birth to the baby. In humans this takes about nine months.

**In hens:** fertilisation is internal, but the embryo develops outside. Soon after fertilisation, the zygote divides repeatedly and travels down the oviduct. As it travels, many protective layers form around it — the hard **shell** is the last. The hen lays the egg; the embryo takes about **3 weeks** to develop into a chick inside, while the hen sits on the eggs to keep them warm. Eggs from a shop are usually unfertilised.

**Viviparous animals** give birth to young ones: humans, cows, dogs, cats.
**Oviparous animals** lay eggs: hens, frogs, lizards, butterflies.

check.why: Once hands, legs, head, eyes and ears are recognisable, the developing embryo is called a foetus.

sections.md:
New individuals that are born or hatched grow into adults. Some animals look very different from their parents when young.

The **frog** life cycle: **egg → tadpole (larva) → adult frog**. A tadpole lives in water, has a tail and gills, and looks more like a fish than a frog! Gradually it grows legs, loses its tail and develops lungs.

The **silkworm** life cycle: **egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (cocoon) → adult moth**. Butterflies follow the same pattern.

The transformation of the larva into an adult through drastic changes is called **metamorphosis**.

In humans, body parts are similar to adults right from birth — we grow bigger, but we do not undergo metamorphosis.

check.why: The silkworm changes drastically from larva to pupa to adult moth, which is metamorphosis.

sections.h: Asexual reproduction: one parent is enough
sections.md:
Look at a drop of pond water with *Hydra* under a microscope. You may see one or more bulges growing out of its body. Each bulge, called a **bud**, develops into a new individual and detaches. Since new individuals develop from buds, this type of asexual reproduction is called **budding**.

**Amoeba** reproduces by **binary fission**. It is a single-celled organism. Its nucleus first divides into two nuclei, then the body divides into two, each part receiving a nucleus. Two amoebae are produced from one parent. 'Binary' means two; 'fission' means splitting.

The type of reproduction in which **only a single parent** is involved is called **asexual reproduction**. Offspring are nearly identical copies of the parent.

**Cloning:** producing an exact copy of a cell, any other living part, or a complete organism. **Dolly the sheep**, born on **5 July 1996** in Scotland (created by Ian Wilmut and colleagues), was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Dolly was identical to the Finn Dorset sheep from which the nucleus came. She died in 2003 from a lung disease. Cloning animals is difficult, and many cloned animals die before birth or soon after.

Two modes: sexual (two parents, fusion of gametes) and asexual (one parent).
Male organs: testes, sperm ducts, penis; testes produce sperms (head, middle piece, tail).
Female organs: ovaries, oviducts, uterus; ovaries release eggs.
Fusion of sperm and egg is fertilisation, forming a zygote.
Internal fertilisation: humans, cows, hens; external: frogs, fish, starfish.
Zygote → embryo (implanted in uterus) → foetus → baby.
Viviparous animals give birth to young; oviparous animals lay eggs.
Metamorphosis: drastic changes from larva to adult, as in frog and silkworm.
Hydra reproduces by budding; Amoeba by binary fission.
Cloning produces an exact copy; Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch06-reproduction.title: Reproduction in Animals — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch06-reproduction.subtitle: Modes of reproduction, reproductive organs, fertilisation, embryo development, viviparous and oviparous animals, metamorphosis and asexual reproduction

sections.md:
Reproduction is essential for the **continuation of a species** — every kind of animal produces young ones like itself. Animals reproduce in two ways:

- **Sexual reproduction:** two parents (male and female); involves the fusion of male and female **gametes**.
- **Asexual reproduction:** only one parent; no gametes fuse.

This chapter studies both, in calm scientific language.

check.q: Sexual reproduction involves…
options: fusion of male and female gametes
check.why: In sexual reproduction, a male gamete and a female gamete fuse, so two parents are involved.

sections.md:
**Male reproductive organs:** a pair of **testes**, two **sperm ducts** and a **penis**. Testes produce male gametes called **sperms**. Millions of sperms are produced; each is a single cell with a **head, a middle piece and a tail**. The tail helps it move.

**Female reproductive organs:** a pair of **ovaries**, **oviducts (fallopian tubes)** and the **uterus**. Ovaries produce female gametes called **ova (eggs)**. In human beings, a single mature egg is released into the oviduct by one of the ovaries every month. The uterus is where the baby develops.

The egg is also a single cell. Gametes vary greatly in size: a human egg is tiny, while a hen's egg (which is also a single cell when formed) is much larger, and an ostrich egg is the largest.

check.q: Which organ in the female produces eggs?
check.why: Ovaries produce the female gametes, the ova or eggs.

sections.md:
The fusion of a sperm with an egg is **fertilisation**. The nuclei of the two fuse to form a single nucleus, giving a **zygote** — the first cell of the new individual. The zygote carries characters from both parents, which is why children resemble both their mother and father in some ways.

**Internal fertilisation** takes place inside the female's body — in humans, cows, dogs and hens.

**External fertilisation** takes place outside the body — common in frogs and fish, which live in water. In spring or the rainy season, frogs and toads go to ponds and streams; the female lays hundreds of eggs in water, covered by a layer of jelly that holds them together and protects them. The male deposits sperms over them. Because eggs and sperms are exposed to water currents, wind and other animals, many are lost — hence so many are produced.

**Test-tube babies (IVF).** When a woman's oviducts are blocked, doctors can collect a freshly released egg and sperms and let them fuse in the laboratory; the zygote is grown for about a week and placed in the mother's uterus. The baby then develops normally. The name is misleading — the baby does not grow in a test tube.

check.q: Fertilisation in frogs is…
check.why: Female frogs lay eggs in water and males deposit sperms over them, so fusion happens outside the body.

sections.md:
The zygote divides repeatedly to form a ball of cells. The cells then begin to form groups that develop into different tissues and organs. This developing structure is an **embryo**.

The embryo gets embedded in the wall of the **uterus** and continues to develop. Body parts such as hands, legs, head, eyes and ears form. The stage of the embryo in which all the body parts can be identified is called a **foetus**. When development is complete, the mother gives birth to the baby.

In **hens**, after internal fertilisation the zygote divides as it travels down the oviduct, and protective layers form around it; the **hard shell** forms last. The hen lays the egg, and the embryo takes about **3 weeks** to develop into a chick while the hen sits on (incubates) the eggs to keep them warm.

In external fertilisation (frogs, fish), the embryo develops outside the female's body, protected by the egg covering.

check.why: Once the main body parts are recognisable, the developing embryo is called a foetus.

sections.h: Viviparous and oviparous animals; young ones to adults
sections.md:
**Viviparous animals** give birth to young ones — human beings, cows, dogs, cats.

**Oviparous animals** lay eggs — hens, frogs, lizards, butterflies, fish.

**Activity idea:** collect eggs of frogs from a pond in the rainy season — eggs laid by birds, frogs and fish look very different.

**From young ones to adults.** Newborns grow into adults. Some animals look very different when young. In the frog's life, **egg → tadpole → adult frog**; in the silk moth, **egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa → adult**. The transformation of a larva into an adult through drastic changes is called **metamorphosis**. Humans do not undergo metamorphosis — body parts are similar from birth to adulthood.

check.q: Which animal is viviparous?
check.why: A cow gives birth to live young ones, so it is viviparous.

sections.h: Asexual reproduction: budding, binary fission and cloning
sections.md:
**Budding in Hydra.** A small bulge (a **bud**) grows on the body of Hydra, develops into a new individual and detaches. Since new individuals develop from buds, this is **budding**.

**Binary fission in Amoeba.** The nucleus divides into two, then the body divides into two, each part getting a nucleus — two Amoebae from one. This is **binary fission**.

Both are types of **asexual reproduction** — only a single parent is involved.

**Cloning.** Producing an exact copy of a cell, any living part or a complete organism. **Dolly the sheep** was the first mammal cloned successfully, by **Ian Wilmut and colleagues** at the Roslin Institute, Scotland; Dolly was born on **5 July 1996**. A nucleus from a mammary-gland cell of a Finn Dorset sheep was put into an egg (with its own nucleus removed) of a Scottish blackface ewe; the egg was placed in the uterus of a blackface ewe. Dolly was identical to the Finn Dorset sheep that gave the nucleus, showing the nucleus carries the characters. Dolly died in 2003. Many cloned animals are born with defects, so cloning is still a subject of research.

check.q: Hydra reproduces asexually by…
check.why: A bud grows on Hydra's body and develops into a new Hydra that separates — budding.

summary: Reproduction continues the species; it is sexual (two parents) or asexual (one parent).
Male organs: testes, sperm ducts, penis; testes make sperms.
Female organs: ovaries, oviducts, uterus; ovaries release eggs.
Fusion of sperm and egg is fertilisation, forming a zygote.
Internal fertilisation: humans, cows, hens. External: frogs, fish.
IVF babies are fertilised outside but grow in the mother's uterus.
Zygote → embryo → foetus; the embryo develops in the uterus wall.
Viviparous animals give birth; oviparous animals lay eggs.
Metamorphosis: dramatic change from larva to adult (frog, silk moth).
Hydra buds; Amoeba divides by binary fission.
Dolly (born 1996) was the first cloned mammal.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence.title: Reaching the Age of Adolescence
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence.subtitle: Why your body and mind are changing — hormones, health and myths, explained calmly

sections.md:
Paheli notices that her kurta from last Diwali is now too short. Boojho's voice cracks in the middle of a sentence and his friends laugh. A classmate who was the shortest in Class 6 is suddenly the tallest. If any of this sounds familiar, welcome — you are in **adolescence**.

Humans can reproduce only after a certain age. The period of life when the body undergoes changes leading to **reproductive maturity** is called **adolescence**. It begins around age **11** and lasts up to **18 or 19**. Since it covers the 'teens' (thirteen to nineteen), adolescents are also called **teenagers**. In girls, adolescence may begin a year or two earlier than in boys, and the timing varies from person to person.

The changes during adolescence that mark **puberty** — the time when the reproductive organs become functional — are the main topic of this chapter. The most important change of puberty is that boys and girls become capable of reproduction. Puberty ends when an adolescent reaches reproductive maturity.

Everyone changes at their own pace. There is no 'right' time, and comparing yourself to friends causes needless worry.

**1. Increase in height.** The most conspicuous change. Long bones — of the arms and legs — elongate and make a person tall. Initially girls grow faster than boys, but by about 18 both reach their maximum height. Height depends on genes inherited from parents, and also on food.

**2. Change in body shape.** Boys develop broader shoulders and a wider chest as muscles grow. In girls, the region below the waist becomes wider.

**3. Voice change.** At puberty, the voice box or **larynx** begins to grow. Boys develop a larger voice box; it can be seen as a protruding part of the throat called the **Adam's apple**. Boys' voices become deeper (sometimes hoarse and cracking for a while). Girls' larynx is smaller and hardly visible; their voice tends to be high-pitched.

**4. Increased activity of sweat and sebaceous (oil) glands.** Many young people get **acne and pimples** on the face because of this. Washing the face regularly helps.

**5. Development of sex organs.** Male sex organs like testes and penis develop completely; testes start producing sperms. In girls, ovaries enlarge and eggs begin to mature; ovaries start releasing mature eggs.

**6. Reaching mental, intellectual and emotional maturity.** Adolescence is also a time when a person's way of thinking changes. You become more independent and self-conscious. Intellectual development is high — the brain has great capacity for learning. Sometimes you may feel insecure while adjusting to the changes. That is normal and temporary.

sections.md:
Some features develop at puberty that help distinguish male from female bodies. These are **secondary sexual characters**:

- In **girls**, breasts begin to develop.
- In **boys**, facial hair — moustache and beard — begins to grow.
- In both, hair grows under the arms and in the genital area. Boys may also develop hair on the chest.

These changes are a natural part of growing up.

What starts all these changes? **Hormones** — chemical substances secreted by **endocrine glands** (ductless glands). They are released **directly into the bloodstream** and reach particular body parts called **target sites**, where they trigger changes.

The onset of puberty is controlled by hormones:

- The **pituitary gland** in the brain releases hormones that stimulate the testes and ovaries.
- **Testes** release the male hormone **testosterone**. It causes the changes in boys — facial hair, deep voice, and so on.
- **Ovaries** produce the female hormone **estrogen**, which makes the breasts develop. Milk-secreting glands develop inside the breasts.

**Other endocrine glands and their hormones:**

head: Gland
Hormone
Main job
rows: Helps the body cope with anger, worry, stress
fig.caption: Endocrine glands release hormones straight into the blood.

check.q: Which hormone requires iodine to be made?
check.why: The thyroid gland uses iodine to make thyroxine; lack of iodine causes goitre.

sections.h: Hormones in other animals; reproductive phase
sections.md:
Hormones control dramatic changes in other animals too. Remember the frog's tadpole? **Thyroxine**, made by the thyroid, controls the change from tadpole to adult frog. If the water lacks iodine, the thyroid cannot make thyroxine and **tadpoles cannot become adults**. Insects too use hormones for metamorphosis.

**Reproductive phase of life:** adolescents become capable of reproduction when their testes and ovaries begin to produce gametes. In **females**, the reproductive phase starts at puberty (10–12 years) and generally lasts till about **45–50 years**.

The ovum matures and one is released by one of the ovaries once in about **28 to 30 days**. During this period the wall of the uterus becomes thick to receive the egg in case it is fertilised. If fertilisation does not occur, the released egg and the thickened lining of the uterus, along with its blood vessels, are shed off. This causes bleeding in women, which is called **menstruation**. It occurs once in about 28–30 days.

The first menstrual flow begins at puberty and is called **menarche**. At 45–50 years, the cycle stops; this is called **menopause**. Initially the cycle may be irregular; it takes time to become regular.

> A period is a normal, healthy body process — never something to be ashamed of. Schools and families should make sanitary products and clean toilets easily available.

sections.h: Boy or girl? How sex is determined
sections.md:
Inside the nucleus of every cell are thread-like **chromosomes**. All human beings have **23 pairs** of chromosomes. Two of these are **sex chromosomes**, named **X and Y**.

- A **female** has **two X** chromosomes (XX).
- A **male** has **one X and one Y** (XY).

The egg always has one X chromosome. A sperm can have either an X or a Y.
- Egg (X) + sperm (X) → **XX → girl**
- Egg (X) + sperm (Y) → **XY → boy**

So the sex of the baby is determined by **whether the fertilising sperm carries X or Y** — that is, by the father's sperm. It is completely wrong and unfair to blame a mother for the birth of a girl or boy. Daughters and sons are equally precious.

In some animals, such as certain reptiles, the temperature at which eggs are kept decides the sex of the young.

options: The sperm, carrying X or Y
check.why: All eggs carry X; an X-carrying sperm gives XX (girl) and a Y-carrying sperm gives XY (boy).

sections.md:
The physical and mental well-being of an individual is regarded as health. To keep the body healthy, every human being, at any age, needs a balanced diet, personal hygiene and adequate physical exercise. In adolescence this is even more important because the body is growing fast.

**Nutritional needs.** A **balanced diet** includes proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals in requisite proportions. Indian meals like **roti, dal, rice and vegetables** are a balanced meal. **Milk** is itself balanced. **Iron** builds blood: leafy vegetables, jaggery, meat, citrus, Indian gooseberry (amla) are good sources. Avoid relying on packaged chips and fizzy drinks; they lack nutrients.

**Personal hygiene.** Bathe at least once a day, especially in hot months, as sweat glands are more active. Clean all parts of the body daily. Girls should take special care during menstruation and change sanitary pads every 4–6 hours or as needed.

**Physical exercise.** Walking, playing outdoor games, yoga and sports keep the body fit and the mind fresh.

**Say NO to drugs.** Adolescents face many doubts and pressures from peers. Drugs are addictive; once taken, a person keeps wanting them. They harm the body and mind and ruin lives. If a friend offers drugs, refuse firmly and talk to a trusted adult. **AIDS** is caused by **HIV**, a virus, which can pass through sexual contact, from an infected mother to her baby through her milk, or through **shared syringes** used for drug injections.

**Myths and taboos.** Many false beliefs exist — that a girl should not look at mirrors during periods, that the mother is responsible for the sex of the baby, that girls should not be allowed to work in the kitchen during periods. These have no scientific basis and should be rejected kindly but firmly.

**Adolescent pregnancy.** In India, the **legal age for marriage** is **18 for girls and 21 for boys**. Early marriage and motherhood cause health problems for mother and child and cut short education and career opportunities.

summary: Adolescence lasts from about 11 to 19 years; puberty is when reproductive organs mature.
Changes: growth spurt, change in body shape, voice change, active sweat and oil glands, development of sex organs, mental and emotional maturity.
Adam's apple is the enlarged larynx in boys.
Secondary sexual characters: breasts in girls; facial hair in boys; body hair in both.
Hormones from endocrine glands travel in blood to target sites.
Testosterone (testes) and estrogen (ovaries) control puberty, under control of the pituitary.
Thyroid—thyroxine (needs iodine); pancreas—insulin; adrenal—adrenalin.
Thyroxine controls tadpole-to-frog metamorphosis.
Menstruation occurs about every 28–30 days; menarche starts it, menopause ends it at 45–50.
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; XX female, XY male; the sperm decides the baby's sex.
Balanced diet, hygiene and exercise keep adolescents healthy; say no to drugs.
Legal marriage age in India: 18 for girls, 21 for boys.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence-.title: Reaching the Age of Adolescence — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence-.subtitle: Puberty changes, secondary sexual characters, hormones, sex determination, endocrine glands, nutrition, hygiene and saying no to drugs

sections.md:
Growth begins at birth, but between about **11 and 19 years** the body changes in special ways. This period of life is **adolescence** — also called **teenage** (thirteen to nineteen). In girls it may begin a year or two earlier than in boys, and its timing varies from person to person.

The body undergoes changes that mark the onset of **puberty**. The most important change is that boys and girls become capable of reproduction. Puberty ends when an adolescent reaches **reproductive maturity**. Everybody's rate of growth is different — there is no 'correct' timing.

**1. Increase in height.** The long bones of the arms and legs elongate, making a person tall. Initially girls grow faster than boys, but by about 18 both reach their maximum height. A rough rule from the chapter: if a boy is 120 cm at 9 years and has reached 75% of his full height, his full height = 120 × 100/75 = **160 cm**.

**2. Change in body shape.** Boys' shoulders broaden and chests widen; muscles grow more prominently. In girls the region below the waist becomes wider.

**3. Voice change.** The **voice box (larynx)** begins to grow. In boys it grows larger and becomes visible as a protruding part of the throat called the **Adam's apple**; the voice becomes hoarse and deeper. In girls the larynx is smaller and hardly visible; their voices are high-pitched. Sometimes a boy's voice 'cracks' while the muscles of the voice box grow.

**4. Increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands.** This can cause **acne and pimples** on the face — wash your face regularly; don't squeeze pimples.

**5. Development of sex organs.** At puberty, male sex organs like the testes and penis develop completely; testes begin to produce sperms. In girls the ovaries enlarge and eggs begin to mature and be released.

**6. Reaching mental, intellectual and emotional maturity.** Adolescents become more independent and self-conscious, their thinking expands, and they may feel unsure or moody at times — this is normal.

check.q: A girl is 140 cm tall at 10 years and has reached 84% of her full height. Her full height will be about…
check.why: Full height = 140 × 100 ÷ 84 ≈ 166.7 cm.

sections.md:
Features that help to distinguish the male from the female, apart from the reproductive organs, are **secondary sexual characters**: in girls, breasts begin to develop; in boys, hair grows on the face (moustache and beard). Both develop hair under the arms and in the pubic region.

These changes are controlled by **hormones** — chemical substances secreted by **endocrine glands** (ductless glands) directly into the **bloodstream**, which carries them to a target site.

- **Testes** release the male hormone **testosterone** at puberty.
- **Ovaries** produce the female hormone **estrogen**, which makes breasts develop and mammary glands form inside.
- The production of these hormones is under the control of another hormone from the **pituitary gland**.

check.q: Hormones are carried to their target sites by…
check.why: Endocrine glands are ductless and pour hormones directly into the blood, which carries them.

sections.md:
Adolescents become capable of reproduction when testes and ovaries begin producing gametes. The reproductive phase lasts much longer in males. In women it begins at puberty (10–12 years) and generally lasts till about **45–50 years**.

The ovum matures and is released by one ovary once in about **28–30 days**. Each month the wall of the uterus thickens to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does not occur, the egg and the thickened lining with its blood vessels are shed — this is **menstruation**, which occurs once in about 28–30 days.

The first menstrual flow at puberty is **menarche**; its stopping at 45–50 years is **menopause**. Cycles may be irregular initially — if worries persist, a doctor should be consulted. The cycle is controlled by hormones.

check.q: The first menstrual flow is called…
check.why: Menarche is the first menstruation at puberty; menopause is when it stops.

sections.h: How is the sex of the baby determined?
sections.md:
Inside the fertilised egg are the instructions that decide the sex. All human beings have **23 pairs of chromosomes** in the nucleus of their cells. Two of these are **sex chromosomes**, named **X and Y**.

- A female has **two X** chromosomes.
- A male has **one X and one Y**.

All eggs carry an X. Sperms are of two kinds: half carry X, half carry Y.

- X sperm + egg → **XX → girl**.
- Y sperm + egg → **XY → boy**.

So the **sex of the child is determined by the father's sperm**, not the mother. Blaming a mother for the sex of a child is scientifically wrong and unfair.

| Egg | Sperm | Zygote | Child |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | X | XX | Girl |
| X | Y | XY | Boy |

check.q: A zygote with XY chromosomes develops into…
check.why: XY means a Y-carrying sperm fertilised the egg, so the child is a boy.

sections.md:
| Gland | Hormone / role |
|---|---|
| **Pituitary** (in the brain) | Growth hormone and hormones that control other glands — called the master gland |
| **Thyroid** (in the neck) | **Thyroxine**; lack of iodine in diet can cause **goitre** (swollen neck) |
| **Pancreas** | **Insulin**; too little causes **diabetes** |
| **Adrenals** (on the kidneys) | **Adrenalin** — helps cope with stress, anger, worry; also keeps salt level in blood correct |
| Testes / Ovaries | Testosterone / estrogen and progesterone |

If the growth hormone from the pituitary is not produced in the right quantity, a person may grow too tall or remain very short.

**Hormones in insects and frogs.** **Metamorphosis** — from caterpillar to moth, tadpole to frog — is controlled by insect hormones and, in frogs, by **thyroxine** from the thyroid; thyroxine production needs **iodine** in water. If pond water lacks iodine, tadpoles cannot become adults.

check.q: Which hormone deficiency is linked with diabetes?
check.why: Insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar; too little insulin causes diabetes.

sections.h: Reproductive health: food, hygiene, exercise and saying no to drugs
sections.md:
**Nutritional needs.** Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, so a **balanced diet** is vital: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals in the right proportion. Indian meals like roti/rice, dal and vegetables form a balanced diet. Milk is a balanced food in itself. **Iron** (leafy vegetables, jaggery, meat, citrus, amla) builds blood; **iodine** (iodised salt) for the thyroid. Avoid relying on chips and packaged snacks.

**Personal hygiene.** Bathe at least once a day, especially in hot weather when sweat glands are active; clean all body parts and wear clean clothes. Girls should keep track of the cycle and use clean sanitary napkins or pads, changing them every 4–5 hours as needed.

**Physical exercise.** Walking, playing outdoors and sport keep the body fit and the mind fresh.

**Say 'NO' to drugs.** Curiosity and peer pressure may tempt some adolescents. Drugs are **addictive**, harm health and happiness, and you may not be able to stop once you start. Avoid them. Also know that **HIV/AIDS** can spread from an infected person through sharing syringes, from an infected mother to the baby, or through sexual contact — so never share needles.

**Myths and facts.** A girl becomes pregnant if she looks at boys during menstruation — **false**. The mother is responsible for the sex of the child — **false**. A girl should not be allowed to work in the kitchen during menstruation — **false**; this is a myth.

**Adolescent pregnancy.** In India, the legal age of marriage is **18 for girls and 21 for boys**. Early marriage and motherhood cause health problems for mother and child and cut short education and employment.

check.q: Which nutrient from iodised salt prevents goitre?
check.why: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; its lack causes the thyroid to swell, called goitre.

summary: Adolescence (about 11–19 years) is when the body changes towards reproductive maturity; puberty marks its onset.
Changes: height, body shape, voice, sweat and sebaceous glands, sex organs, and emotional maturity.
Adam's apple is the enlarged larynx in boys.
Secondary sexual characters include beard in boys and breasts in girls.
Testosterone (testes) and estrogen (ovaries) are controlled by pituitary hormones.
Menstruation occurs every 28–30 days; menarche begins it, menopause ends it.
Females are XX, males XY; the father's sperm determines the child's sex.
Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenals, testes, ovaries.
Lack of iodine causes goitre; lack of insulin causes diabetes.
Thyroxine (needs iodine) controls metamorphosis in tadpoles.
Balanced diet, hygiene, exercise and avoiding drugs keep adolescents healthy.
Legal age of marriage in India: 18 for girls, 21 for boys.

rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.title: Force and Pressure
rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.subtitle: Pushes, pulls, sharp knives, camel feet and the invisible weight of the air on your head

sections.h: Every action is a push or a pull
sections.md:
Watch a cricket match for a minute. The bowler swings his arm and the ball leaves his hand. The batter swings and the ball reverses direction. A fielder dives and stops it dead. The ball speeds up, changes direction, stops — and every change is caused by something pushing or pulling it.

In science, **a push or a pull on an object is called a force**. Opening a door, kicking a football, lifting a school bag, pulling a bucket from a well, squeezing toothpaste — all involve force.

**Forces are due to an interaction.** At least **two objects must interact** for a force to come into play. A man pushing a stationary car is applying a force; if he stops touching it, there's no force from him. In a tug-of-war, two teams pull a rope in opposite directions.

**Exploring forces:**
- Forces applied on an object **in the same direction add** to one another.
- If two forces act in **opposite directions**, the net force is the **difference** between the two, and the object moves in the direction of the larger force.
- If equal forces act in opposite directions, the net force is zero and nothing moves — like an evenly matched tug-of-war.

The strength of a force is expressed by its **magnitude**. Force also has a **direction**. If either changes, its effect changes. The SI unit of force is the **newton (N)**.
