check.q: Why were forest villages set up?
options: To ensure a steady supply of cheap labour for the forest department
check.why: People were allowed to live in forest villages only if they worked for the forest department cutting trees and protecting forests.

sections.h: The problem with trade, and the search for work
sections.md:
During the 19th century tribal groups found that **traders and moneylenders** were coming into the forests more often, wanting to buy forest produce, offering cash loans, and asking them to work for wages. It took tribal groups some time to understand what was happening.

**Silk growers**: In the 18th century, Indian silk was in demand in European markets. The fine quality of Indian silk was highly valued and exports from India increased rapidly. As the market expanded, East India Company officials tried to encourage silk production to meet the growing demand. **Hazaribagh**, in present-day Jharkhand, was an area where the **Santhals** reared **cocoons**. The traders dealing in silk sent in their agents who gave loans to the tribal people and collected the cocoons. The growers were paid **Rs 3 to 4 for a thousand cocoons**. These were then exported to **Burdwan or Gaya** where they were sold at **five times the price**. The middlemen — so called because they arranged deals between the exporters and silk growers — made huge profits. The silk growers earned very little. Understandably, many tribal groups saw the market and the traders as their main enemies.

**Worked check:** if a middleman buys 1,000 cocoons for Rs 4 and sells them for five times as much, he sells for 5 × 4 = Rs 20, so he keeps Rs 16 — four times what the grower got.

**The search for work**: The plight of the tribals who had to go far away from their homes in search of work was even worse. From the late 19th century, **tea plantations** started coming up and **mining** became an important industry. Tribals were recruited in large numbers to work the tea plantations of **Assam** and the **coal mines of Jharkhand**. They were recruited through **contractors** who paid them miserably low wages, and prevented them from returning home.

check.q: How much did Santhal cocoon growers get for 1,000 cocoons?
check.why: Traders paid only about Rs 3–4 for a thousand cocoons and then sold them for around five times the price.

sections.h: A closer look: Birsa Munda's movement
sections.md:
Birsa was born in the **mid-1870s**. The son of a poor father, he grew up around the forests of **Bohonda**, grazing sheep, playing the flute, and dancing in the local *akhara*. Forced by poverty, his father had to move from place to place looking for work.

As a boy Birsa heard tales of the Munda uprisings of the past and saw the **sirdars** (leaders) of the community urging the people to revolt. They talked of a golden age when the Mundas had been free of the oppression of dikus, and of a time when the ancestral right of the community would be restored. They saw themselves as the descendants of the original settlers of the region.

Birsa went to the local **missionary school**, and listened to the sermons of missionaries. There too he heard it said that it was possible for the Mundas to attain the Kingdom of Heaven, and regain their lost rights — if they became good Christians and gave up their 'bad practices'. Later Birsa also spent some time in the company of a prominent **Vaishnav** preacher. He wore the sacred thread, and began to value the importance of purity and piety.

**Birsa's message**: He urged the Mundas to give up drinking liquor, clean their village, and stop believing in witchcraft and sorcery. He also turned against missionaries and Hindu landlords. He talked of a **golden age** in the past — a *satyug* (the age of truth) — when Mundas lived a good life, constructed embankments, tapped natural springs, planted trees and orchards, practised cultivation to earn their living. In that imagined past, Mundas did not kill their brethren and relatives. They lived honestly. Birsa also wanted people to once again work on their land, settle down and cultivate their fields.

**Political aim**: What worried British officials most was the political aim of the movement: to drive out missionaries, moneylenders, Hindu landlords and the government, and to set up a **Munda Raj** with Birsa at its head. The movement identified all these forces as the cause of the misery the Mundas were suffering. The land policies of the British were destroying their traditional land system; Hindu landlords and moneylenders were taking over their land; and missionaries were criticising their traditional culture.

**British response**: In **1895** Birsa was arrested and convicted on charges of rioting and was jailed for **two years**. When he was released in **1897** he began touring the villages to gather support. He used traditional symbols and language to rouse people, urging them to destroy 'Ravana' (dikus and the Europeans) and establish a kingdom under his leadership. Birsa's followers began targeting the symbols of diku and European power. They attacked **police stations and churches**, and raided the property of **moneylenders and zamindars**. They raised the **white flag** as a symbol of Birsa Raj.

In **1900 Birsa died of cholera** and the movement faded out.

**Why it mattered**:
- It forced the colonial government to introduce laws so that the land of the tribals could not be easily taken over by dikus (the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908**).
- It showed once again that the tribal people had the capacity to protest against injustice and express their anger against colonial rule. They did this in their own specific way, inventing their own rituals and symbols of struggle.

sections.md:
Birsa Munda is remembered as **'Dharti Aaba'** (Father of the Earth) by many in Jharkhand. The state of **Jharkhand** was formed on **15 November 2000** — on his birth anniversary — and since 2021 the Government of India marks 15 November as **Janjatiya Gaurav Divas** (Tribal Pride Day). His portrait hangs in the Central Hall of Parliament.

**Thinking question**: Why do you think Birsa spoke of a 'golden age' in the past? When people face great hardship, memories — real or imagined — of a better past can inspire hope and unity. Birsa's golden age was not just nostalgia: it was a picture of how life ought to be — land in the hands of those who worked it, villages clean and sober, no exploitation by outsiders.

**Activity**: Find out about one tribal community in your state today. What are its main occupations? What problems related to land and forests does it face? Has any law (for example, the Forest Rights Act, 2006) affected it?

check.q: Which state was formed on Birsa Munda's birth anniversary?
check.why: Jharkhand was created on 15 November 2000, the anniversary of Birsa Munda's birth.

story.title: The Flute and the White Flag — an imagined evening in a Munda village, 1898

parts.md: Somra was twelve, and his job was to graze the goats near the sal forest. Last year a forest guard had told his uncle that the patch where the family used to burn and sow was now 'Reserved'. Uncle had argued; the guard had written something in a book. Since then, uncle went to cut logs for the forest office three days a week — the price of being allowed to live in the forest village.

Somra's mother reared silk cocoons. When the trader's agent came, he counted them quickly, pressed a few coins into her hand and loaded the basket onto his bullock cart. 'In Gaya,' whispered Somra's cousin, who had been there, 'these sell for five times as much.' Mother said nothing. She still owed the moneylender for last year's seed.

That evening a man arrived in the village akhara, dusty from walking. The elders said he had been with Birsa. He spoke of a time when the Mundas had planted orchards and built embankments, when no diku could take their land. He told them to stop drinking, to keep the village clean, and to stand together. Somra played his flute softly at the back; the old women hummed.

Some weeks later, Somra saw young men carrying a white flag along the forest path. People said the police station near Khunti had been attacked. His mother was frightened; his uncle was proud. Nobody slept well.

In 1900 the news came: Birsa had died in jail, of cholera. The village mourned. But years later, when Somra was a grown man, a new law was read out by the patwari: tribal land could not be easily bought by outsiders. Somra thought of the white flag and the stranger in the akhara, and played the old tune on his flute once more.

summary: Birsa Munda (born mid-1870s) led a movement in Chotanagpur in the 1890s; Mundas, Oraons and Santhals followed.

rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-ch05-when-peo.title: When People Rebel: 1857 and After
rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-ch05-when-peo.subtitle: How a rumour about cartridges lit a fire that spread from Meerut to Lucknow — and changed how India was ruled

sections.md:
Imagine the cantonment at Meerut on a hot May evening in 1857. Church bells are ringing for Sunday service. Suddenly, Indian soldiers — *sepoys* — break open the jail, free eighty-five comrades who had been chained and humiliated the day before, and turn their guns on their British officers. By the next morning, they have ridden about 60 km to Delhi and are asking an old poet-king, Bahadur Shah Zafar, to lead them.

How did a dispute over rifle cartridges become one of the largest uprisings against colonial rule anywhere in the nineteenth century? To answer that, we must step back and see how the East India Company's policies had, over a hundred years, angered almost every group in north India: kings and queens, nawabs, landlords, peasants and soldiers.

This chapter follows that story in four steps:

1. **Policies and the people** — how Company rule hurt different groups.
2. **A mutiny becomes a popular rebellion** — how it spread.
3. **The Company fights back** — how it was crushed.
4. **Aftermath** — how British rule changed after 1858.

> Keep one question in mind as you read: *Why did so many different people join in at the same time?*

From the mid-eighteenth century, rulers in India watched their power shrink. The Company placed **Residents** at their courts, cut down their armies, took away their revenues and, finally, their territories.

Many ruling families tried to negotiate. **Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi** wanted the Company to accept her adopted son as heir after her husband died. **Nana Saheb**, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, asked for his father's pension to continue. The Company refused both.

The main tool behind these refusals was Lord Dalhousie's **Doctrine of Lapse** (from 1848): if a ruler died without a male heir *born to him*, the kingdom would 'lapse' and become Company territory. Satara (1848), Sambalpur, Udaipur, Nagpur and Jhansi were taken over this way.

**Awadh** was different. It was annexed in **1856** on the charge of 'misgovernment', and Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was sent to Calcutta. This hurt deeply, because Awadh was the home of many sepoys.

The Mughal emperor too was squeezed. The Company had removed the emperor's name from the coins it minted (from 1835). In 1849 Dalhousie announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar's death the family would have to leave the Red Fort and move elsewhere. In 1856 Governor-General Canning declared that Zafar would be the last Mughal 'king'; after his death none of his descendants would be recognised as kings — they would just be called princes.
keyTerms: Resident — Company official posted at an Indian court
Doctrine of Lapse — rule that a kingdom without a natural male heir passes to the Company
Annexation — taking over another's territory

check.q: On what ground was Awadh annexed in 1856?
check.why: Awadh's nawab had heirs, so the Company used the charge of 'misgovernment' instead of the Doctrine of Lapse.

sections.h: The problem of the peasants and the sepoys
sections.md:
Away from the palaces, ordinary people had their own grievances.

**Peasants and zamindars** in the countryside resented the high taxes and the rigid methods of revenue collection. Many failed to pay back their loans to the moneylenders and gradually lost the lands they had tilled for generations.

**Sepoys** in the employ of the Company had their own reasons for discontent. They were unhappy about their **pay, allowances and conditions of service**. Some of the new rules violated their religious sensibilities and beliefs. In those days many people in the country believed that if they crossed the sea they would lose their religion and caste. So when in **1824** sepoys were told to go to **Burma** by the sea route to fight for the Company, they refused to follow the order, though they agreed to go by the land route. They were severely punished, and since the issue did not die down, in **1856** the Company passed a new law which stated that every new person who took up employment in the Company's army had to agree to **serve overseas** if required.

Sepoys also reacted to what was happening in the countryside. Many of them were **peasants** and had families living in the villages. So the anger of the peasants quickly spread among the sepoys.

sections.md:
The British believed that Indian society had to be reformed. Laws were passed to stop the practice of **sati** (1829) and to encourage the **remarriage of widows** (1856). **English-language education** was actively promoted. After 1830, the Company allowed **Christian missionaries** to function freely in its domain and even own land and property. In **1850**, a new law was passed to make conversion to Christianity easier: it allowed an Indian who had converted to Christianity to **inherit the property of his ancestors**.

Many Indians began to feel that the British were destroying their religion, their social customs and their traditional way of life.

Of course there were other Indians who wanted to change existing social practices — reformers like Raja Rammohun Roy and Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, whom you will meet in a later chapter. Society was divided; but in 1857 the fear of interference was widespread.

> **Did you know?** Some reforms we now see as just — like banning sati — were seen by many at the time as interference. History asks us to understand *why* people felt as they did, not only to judge them.

check.q: What did the law of 1850 do?
options: Allowed a convert to Christianity to inherit ancestral property
check.why: The 1850 law let converts inherit ancestral property, making conversion easier and deepening fears about religion.

sections.h: Through the eyes of the people: rumours and prophecies
sections.md:
Before the revolt, north India was full of **rumours** — and rumours spread fast when people are already anxious.

- People said the British had mixed the **bone dust of cows and pigs** into flour sold in the market to destroy caste and religion.
- In the months before May 1857, **chapatis** were passed from village to village in many parts of north India, mysteriously, at night. No one fully knows what they meant; British officials were alarmed, and many villagers read them as a sign of coming upheaval.
- A **prophecy** went around that British rule would end on the **hundredth anniversary of the Battle of Plassey** — 23 June 1857.
- Religious leaders like **Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah** of Faizabad openly preached that British rule would soon end.

Historians treat rumours as **evidence**: not of what was true, but of what people **feared and believed**. A rumour that the cartridges were greased with forbidden fat spread so quickly because people already believed the Company wanted to attack their faith.

**Box — a proclamation.** During the revolt, rebel leaders issued proclamations in the name of the Mughal emperor, appealing to both **Hindus and Muslims** to unite against the British, and listing the grievances of zamindars, merchants, artisans, soldiers and religious men. The fact that the rebels addressed so many groups shows how wide the anger was.

check.q: Why do historians study rumours like the one about the cartridges?
options: Because they show what people feared and believed
check.why: Rumours are evidence of popular fears and beliefs, explaining why people acted as they did.

sections.md:
A **mutiny** is when soldiers collectively disobey officers. In 1857 a mutiny grew into a mass rebellion.

**The spark: cartridges.** On 29 March 1857, young sepoy **Mangal Pandey** attacked his officers at **Barrackpore** and was hanged. Soon after, sepoys at Meerut refused to do army drill using new cartridges for the Enfield rifle, which were suspected of being coated with the fat of cows and pigs — offensive to both Hindus and Muslims. Eighty-five sepoys were dismissed and sentenced to ten years in jail for disobeying their officers (on 9 May).

**10 May 1857:** Meerut sepoys marched to the jail, released the imprisoned sepoys, attacked and killed British officers, captured guns and ammunition and set fire to buildings, then marched to Delhi. On **11 May** they reached the Red Fort and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** their leader. The old emperor accepted this demand and wrote letters to all the chiefs and rulers of the country to come forward and organise a confederacy of Indian states to fight the British.

**The rebellion spreads.** Once the Mughal emperor gave his name, the revolt gained a symbol. Regiment after regiment mutinied and took off to join other troops at nodal points like Delhi, **Kanpur** and **Lucknow**. After them, the people of the towns and villages also rose up in rebellion and rallied around local leaders, zamindars and chiefs who were prepared to establish their authority and fight the British.

**Leaders emerged:**
- **Nana Saheb** gathered armed forces, expelled the British garrison from Kanpur and proclaimed himself Peshwa, governing under the emperor.
- **Birjis Qadr**, son of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, was proclaimed Nawab in Lucknow; his mother **Begum Hazrat Mahal** took an active part in organising the uprising.
- **Rani Lakshmibai** joined the rebel sepoys in Jhansi and fought the British along with **Tantia Tope**, the general of Nana Saheb.
- In the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh, **Rani Avantibai Lodhi** of Ramgarh raised an army of four thousand and led it against the British.
- **Ahmadullah Shah**, a maulvi from Faizabad, raised a huge force of supporters and came to Lucknow.
- **Bakht Khan**, a soldier from Bareilly, led a large force of fighters who came to Delhi and became a key military leader.
- In Bihar, an old zamindar, **Kunwar Singh**, joined the rebel sepoys and battled the British for many months.

The British were badly outnumbered for a while. Their rule in large parts of north India seemed to collapse.

sections.md:
The Company decided to repress the revolt with all its might. It brought reinforcements from England, passed new laws so that the rebels could be convicted with ease, and then moved into the storm centres of the revolt.

- **Delhi** was recaptured from the rebel forces in **September 1857**. The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was tried in court and sentenced to life imprisonment. He and his wife Begum Zinat Mahal were sent to prison in **Rangoon** (now Yangon, Myanmar) in October 1858. Bahadur Shah Zafar died in the Rangoon jail in November 1862. His sons were shot before his eyes, according to accounts of the time.
- The recapture of Delhi, however, did not mean that the rebellion died down. People continued to resist and battle the British. The British had to fight for **two years** to suppress the massive forces of popular rebellion.
- **Lucknow** was taken in **March 1858**.
- **Rani Lakshmibai** was defeated and killed in **June 1858**.
- **Rani Avantibai**, after losing a battle at Kheri, chose to embrace death rather than surrender.
- **Tantia Tope** escaped to the jungles of central India and continued to fight a guerrilla war with the support of many tribal and peasant leaders. He was captured, tried and killed in **April 1859**.

Just as victories against the British had earlier encouraged rebellion, the defeat of rebel forces encouraged desertions. The British also tried their best to win back the loyalty of the people. They announced rewards for loyal landholders that they would be allowed to continue to enjoy traditional rights over their lands. Those who had rebelled were told that if they submitted to the British, and if they had not killed any white people, they would remain safe and their rights and claims to land would not be denied. Nevertheless, hundreds of sepoys, rebels, nawabs and rajas were tried and hanged.

**Why did the revolt fail?** Historians point to several reasons: the British had better weapons, communications (the telegraph) and money; many rulers, and regions like Punjab and much of the south, did not join; and the rebels lacked a single plan and command. Historians still debate how far it was a 'national' movement — but they agree it was far more than a soldiers' mutiny.

sections.h: Aftermath: a new way of ruling
sections.md:
The British had regained control of the country by the end of 1859, but they could not carry on ruling the land with the same policies any more. The important changes:

1. **Government of India Act 1858** — the powers of the East India Company were transferred to the **British Crown** for ensuring a more responsible management of Indian affairs. A member of the British cabinet was appointed **Secretary of State for India** and made responsible for all matters related to the governance of India. He was given a council to advise him, called the India Council. The Governor-General of India was given the title of **Viceroy**, that is, a personal representative of the Crown. Through these measures, the British government accepted direct responsibility for ruling India.
2. **Ruling chiefs were reassured**: all ruling chiefs of the country were assured that their territory would never be annexed in future. They were allowed to pass on their kingdoms to their heirs, including **adopted sons**. However, they were made to acknowledge the British Queen as their **Sovereign Paramount**. Thus the Indian rulers were to hold their kingdoms as subordinates of the British Crown.
3. **The army was reorganised**: the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army would be reduced and the number of European soldiers would be increased. It was also decided that instead of recruiting soldiers from Awadh, Bihar, central India and south India, more soldiers would be recruited from among the **Gurkhas, Sikhs and Pathans**.
4. **Muslims were treated with suspicion**: the land and property of Muslims were confiscated on a large scale and they were treated with suspicion and hostility. The British believed that they were responsible for the rebellion in a big way.
5. **Respect for religion and customs**: the British decided to respect the customary religious and social practices of the people in India.
6. **Landlords and zamindars** were protected: policies were made to protect landlords and zamindars and give them security of rights over their lands.

Thus a new phase of history began after 1857.

> **Did you know?** The Queen's proclamation of 1 November 1858 was read out at towns across India — a public announcement that a new era of 'Crown rule' had begun.

sections.md:
1857 was not the only uprising of its time. In the 1850s the **Taiping Rebellion** shook China, and in Africa and elsewhere people resisted colonial powers. Comparing them reminds us that colonial rule faced resistance across the world.

In India, 1857 lives on in songs, folk tales, paintings and later nationalist writing. Some British writers of the time called it the 'Sepoy Mutiny', a label that hides the role of peasants, artisans and rulers. Many Indians later called it the **First War of Independence**. Each name tells you something about who is telling the story.

**How do historians know?** They read proclamations issued by rebel leaders, British official letters and reports, newspapers, diaries, petitions, and paintings and photographs. Pictures made by British artists often showed the British as heroic and the rebels as savage; Indian paintings and later posters made Rani Lakshmibai a hero on horseback. Reading such sources critically is the historian's craft.

> **Think:** If you were writing a school book in 1860 in London, and another in 1947 in Delhi, how would your titles for 1857 differ?

story.title: The Drummer Boy of Meerut — an imagined account

parts.md: Ramdeen was fifteen and beat the drum for the 3rd Light Cavalry at Meerut. His father had been a sepoy too; his uncle farmed a small plot near Faizabad in Awadh. In 1856 a letter arrived from the village: the Nawab was gone, the new revenue men had raised the demand, and uncle had borrowed from the moneylender. Ramdeen read it to the older troopers. Many of them had letters just like it.

Then came the new cartridges. 'Bite the end,' the drill sergeant said. In the lines that night, men whispered that the paper was greased with cow and pig fat. Hindus and Muslims alike were horrified. 'They want to break our caste and our faith,' said an old naik. On 9 May, Ramdeen stood on parade and watched eighty-five men stripped of their uniforms and shackled for refusing. Some of them were weeping with shame.

The next evening the bazaar buzzed. Then shots. Troopers ran to the jail, broke the locks and freed their comrades. Smoke rose over the officers' bungalows. Ramdeen, terrified, hid behind the drum store until a friend pulled him onto a horse. All night they rode towards Delhi under the stars.

At dawn on 11 May they reached the Red Fort. Ramdeen saw an old man in white at a window — the emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, a poet more than a soldier. After hours of argument, the emperor agreed to give his name to the cause. Within days, news came of risings in other cantonments. For a summer it seemed the world had turned upside down.

By September British guns were pounding Delhi's walls. Ramdeen escaped east with a band of sepoys and later joined Kunwar Singh's men in Bihar. When it was all over, he went back to his uncle's village, hiding his uniform in a trunk. In 1858, at the district town, he heard a man read the Queen's proclamation: the Company was gone, the Crown would rule. 'Different masters,' said his uncle, 'same revenue man.' Ramdeen was not so sure. Something had changed: people had learned that the Company could be challenged.

rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-civilising-na.title: Civilising the "Native", Educating the Nation
rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-civilising-na.subtitle: Who decides what you learn in school — and why it mattered so much under colonial rule

sections.h: A question about your own school
sections.md:
Think about your timetable: periods, a bell, a fixed syllabus, exams, report cards, a classroom with rows of benches. It feels as natural as the monsoon. But two hundred years ago, most Indian children who studied did so in a very different way — with a guru under a tree, in a small *pathshala* in a rich man's verandah, or in a madrasa attached to a mosque.

Why did that change? The British in India did not only want land and revenue. Many believed they had a cultural mission: they had to **'civilise the natives'** — change their customs and values. Education was a key tool. This chapter asks:

- What did the British think about Indian learning?
- How did their policies change the local schools?
- How did Indians — Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore among them — respond and imagine a *national* education?

> Notice the inverted commas around "Native" in the title. The word was used by the British to suggest people who were primitive. Historians put it in quotes to show that it was *their* label, not a fair description.

sections.h: How the British saw education: the tradition of Orientalism
sections.md:
In 1783 a young linguist, **William Jones**, arrived in Calcutta as a junior judge in the Supreme Court that the Company had set up. Besides being an expert in law, Jones had studied Greek, Latin, French, English, Arabic and Persian. In Calcutta he began spending many hours a day with pandits who taught him the subtleties of the **Sanskrit** language, grammar and poetry. Soon he was studying ancient Indian texts on law, philosophy, religion, politics, morality, arithmetic, medicine and the other sciences.

Jones discovered that his interests were shared by many British officials living in Calcutta at the time. Englishmen like **Henry Thomas Colebrooke** and **Nathaniel Halhed** were also busy discovering the ancient Indian heritage, mastering Indian languages and translating Sanskrit and Persian works into English. Together with them, Jones set up the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** and started a journal called *Asiatick Researches*. Those who studied Asian languages and cultures came to be called **Orientalists**.

Their thinking had two sides:
1. They felt a deep respect for ancient cultures, both of India and the West. Indian civilisation, they felt, had attained its glory in the ancient past, but had subsequently **declined**. To understand India it was necessary to discover the sacred and legal texts produced in the ancient period.
2. They believed that British rule would be accepted if the Company respected and promoted Indian learning — the British could become the **guardians of Indian culture** as well as its masters. Indians would be taught in their own languages, through their own classical texts.

On this basis:
- A **madrasa** was set up in **Calcutta in 1781** to promote the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law.
- The **Hindu College in Benares** was established in **1791** to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts that would be useful for the administration of the country.
keyTerms: Orientalist — scholar who studies the languages and cultures of Asia
Asiatic Society — learned body founded in Calcutta in 1784
Madrasa — institution of learning, often Islamic

sections.h: 'Grave errors of the East': the critics
sections.md:
Not everyone agreed. From the early nineteenth century many British officials began to criticise the Orientalist vision of learning. They said that knowledge of the East was full of errors and unscientific thought; Eastern literature was non-serious and light-hearted. So they argued that it was wrong on the part of the British to spend so much effort in encouraging the study of Arabic and Sanskrit language and literature.

**James Mill** was one of those who attacked the Orientalists. The British effort, he declared, should not be to teach what the natives wanted, or what they respected, in order to please them and 'win a place in their heart'. The aim of education ought to be to teach what was **useful and practical**. So Indians should be made familiar with the scientific and technical advances that the West had made, rather than with the poetry and sacred literature of the Orient.

The most famous critic was **Thomas Babington Macaulay**. He saw India as an uncivilised country that needed to be civilised. No branch of Eastern knowledge, according to him, could be compared to what England had produced. In his **Minute on Indian Education (1835)** he dismissed Indian learning with arrogance, claiming that a single shelf of a good European library was worth more than the whole native literature of India and Arabia. He urged that the British government in India stop wasting public money in promoting Oriental learning, for it was of no practical use. Teaching **English**, he felt, would allow Indians to read some of the finest literature the world had produced; it would make them aware of developments in Western science and philosophy — and would be a way of civilising people, changing their tastes, values and culture.

Following Macaulay's minute, the **English Education Act of 1835** was introduced. The decision was to make English the medium of instruction for higher education, and to stop the promotion of Oriental institutions like the Calcutta Madrasa and Benares Sanskrit College. These institutions were seen as 'temples of darkness that were falling of themselves into decay'. English textbooks now began to be produced for schools.

> **Did you know?** Macaulay himself admitted he knew neither Sanskrit nor Arabic — yet he judged their entire literatures. Ask yourself: can anyone fairly judge a culture they have not studied?

points: Respect for ancient Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic texts
Teach Indians in their own learning

sections.md:
In **1854**, the Court of Directors of the East India Company in London sent an educational despatch to the Governor-General in India. Issued by **Charles Wood**, the President of the Board of Control of the Company, it has come to be known as **Wood's Despatch**. Outlining the educational policy that was to be followed in India, it emphasised once again the practical benefits of a system of European learning, as opposed to Oriental knowledge.

- **For trade and commerce:** European learning would enable Indians to recognise the advantages that flow from the expansion of trade and commerce, and make them see the importance of developing the resources of the country. Introducing them to European ways of life would change their tastes and desires, and create a demand for **British goods**, for Indians would begin to appreciate and buy things produced in Europe.
- **For morality:** it would improve the moral character of Indians. It would make them truthful and honest, and thus supply the Company with **civil servants** who could be trusted and depended upon.

The literature of the East was not only full of grave errors, it could not instil in people a sense of duty and a commitment to work, nor could it develop the skills required for administration.

**What followed:**
- **Education departments** of the government were set up to extend control over all matters regarding education.
- Steps were taken to establish a system of **university education**. In **1857**, while the sepoys rose in revolt in Meerut and Delhi, universities were being established in **Calcutta, Madras and Bombay**.
- Attempts were also made to bring about changes within the system of **school education**.

**Box — what happened to the missionaries?** Until 1813 the East India Company was opposed to missionary activities in India, fearing they would provoke reactions and make people suspicious of British presence. So **William Carey** and other missionaries set up a mission at **Serampore**, which was under the control of the Danish East India Company, in **1800**. They established a printing press in 1800 and a college in 1818. Through the 19th century missionaries set up schools all over the country. After 1857, the British government in India was worried that any direct attack on local customs, practices, beliefs and religious ideas might enrage 'native' public opinion — so it became reluctant to support missionary education directly.

sections.h: What happened to the local schools?
sections.md:
In the 1830s, **William Adam**, a Scottish missionary, toured the districts of Bengal and Bihar. He had been asked by the Company to report on the progress of education in vernacular schools. He found over **1 lakh pathshalas** with more than **20 lakh children** studying in them. These were small institutions with no more than 20 students each — but the total number of children being taught was significant.

How did a pathshala work?
- They were set up by wealthy people, or the local community. At times they were started by a teacher (guru).
- The system was **flexible**: there were no fixed fees, no printed books, no separate school building, no benches or chairs, no blackboards, no system of separate classes, no roll-call registers, no annual examinations, and no regular time-table.
- In some places classes were held under a banyan tree, in other places in the corner of a village shop or temple, or at the guru's home.
- Fees depended on the income of parents: the rich had to pay more than the poor.
- Teaching was **oral**, and the guru decided what to teach, in accordance with the needs of the students. Students were not separated into different classes: all of them sat together in one place. The guru interacted separately with groups of children with different levels of learning.
- Adam discovered that this flexible system was suited to local needs. For instance, classes were **not held during harvest time** when rural children often worked in the fields. The pathshala started once again when the crops had been cut and stored. This meant that even children of peasant families could study.

**New routines, new rules.** Up to the mid-19th century, the Company was concerned primarily with higher education. So it allowed the local pathshalas to function without much interference. After **1854** the Company decided to improve the system of vernacular education. It felt that this could be done by introducing order within the system, imposing routines, establishing rules, ensuring regular inspections.

How was this to be done? The Company appointed a number of **government pandits**, each in charge of looking after **four to five schools**. The task of the pandit was to visit the pathshalas and try and improve the standard of teaching. Each guru was asked to submit periodic reports and take classes according to a regular timetable. Teaching was now to be based on **textbooks** and learning was to be tested through a system of **annual examination**. Students were asked to pay a regular fee, attend regular classes, sit on fixed seats, and obey the new rules of discipline.

Pathshalas which accepted the new rules were supported through **government grants**. Those who were unwilling to work within the new system received no government support. Over time gurus who wanted to retain their independence found it difficult to compete with the government-aided and regulated pathshalas.

The new rules had another consequence. In the earlier system children from poor peasant families had been able to go to pathshalas, since the timetable was flexible. The discipline of the new system demanded **regular attendance**, even during harvest time when children of poor families had to work in the fields. Inability to attend school came to be seen as indiscipline, as evidence of the lack of desire to learn.

sections.h: The agenda for a national education
sections.md:
British officials were not the only people thinking about education in India. From the early nineteenth century many thinkers from different parts of India began to talk of the need for a wider spread of education. Impressed with the developments in Europe, some Indians felt that Western education would help modernise India. They urged the British to open more schools, colleges and universities, and spend more money on education. You will read about some of these efforts in the chapter on 'Women, Caste and Reform'. There were other Indians, however, who reacted against Western education. Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore were two such individuals.

**Mahatma Gandhi: 'English education has enslaved us'.** Gandhi argued that colonial education created a sense of **inferiority** in the minds of Indians. It made them see Western civilisation as superior, and destroyed the pride they had in their own culture. There was poison in this education, said Mahatma Gandhi; it was sinful, it enslaved Indians, it cast an evil spell on them. Charmed by the West, appreciating everything that came from the West, Indians educated in these institutions began admiring British rule. Mahatma Gandhi wanted an education that could help Indians recover their sense of **dignity and self-respect**.
- During the national movement he urged students to leave educational institutions in order to show to the British that Indians were no longer willing to be enslaved.
- He strongly felt that **Indian languages** ought to be the medium of teaching. Education in English crippled Indians, distanced them from their own social surroundings, and made them 'strangers in their own lands'. Speaking a foreign tongue, despising local culture, the English educated did not know how to relate to the masses.
- Western education, he said, focused on reading and writing rather than oral knowledge; it valued textbooks rather than lived experience and practical knowledge. Education ought to develop a person's mind and soul. **Literacy** — or simply learning to read and write — by itself **did not count as education**. People had to work with their hands, learn a craft, and know how different things operated. This would develop their mind and their capacity to understand.

**Rabindranath Tagore: 'abode of peace'.** As a child, Tagore hated going to school. He found it suffocating and oppressive. The school appeared like a prison, for he could never do what he felt like doing. So while other children listened to the teacher, Tagore's mind would wander away. Tagore wanted to set up a school where the child was happy, where she could be free and creative, where she was able to explore her own thoughts and desires. He felt that childhood ought to be a time of **self-learning**, outside the rigid and restricting discipline of the schooling system set up by the British. Teachers had to be imaginative, understand the child, and help the child develop her curiosity. According to Tagore, the existing schools killed the natural desire of the child to be creative, her sense of wonder.
- He set up his institution in **1901** at **Santiniketan**, about 100 km away from Calcutta, in a rural setting. He saw it as an abode of peace (the literal meaning of *santiniketan*), where living in harmony with nature, children could cultivate their natural creativity.
- Tagore valued combining elements of modern Western civilisation with what he saw as the best within Indian tradition. He emphasised the need to teach **science and technology** at Santiniketan, along with **art, music and dance**.
- Santiniketan later grew into **Visva-Bharati**.

In many senses Gandhi and Tagore thought about education in similar ways. There were, however, differences too. Gandhi was highly critical of Western civilisation and its worship of machines and technology. Tagore wanted to combine elements of modern Western civilisation with what he saw as the best within Indian tradition.

Thus, many individuals and thinkers were thinking of how to educate the nation. After independence, these questions continued to be debated.

left.title: Gandhi
points: Learning by doing; crafts and hand-work

right.title: Tagore
points: Blend Western science with Indian tradition

check.q: What did Tagore believe about childhood learning?
options: It should be a time of self-learning in a free, natural setting
check.why: Tagore set up Santiniketan so children could learn freely, creatively and close to nature rather than in prison-like schools.

sections.md:
Many of today's debates began in this period. Should children learn first in their mother tongue? Should schools teach crafts and skills alongside books? How much should exams decide a child's future? India's present education policies, which encourage early learning in the home language and vocational skills from middle school, echo questions that Gandhi, Tagore and even the Orientalists argued about.

The history of education also shows how **knowledge and power** are linked. Whoever writes the syllabus decides what counts as 'knowledge' and whose culture is shown as superior. A colonial system that called Indian learning 'error' was also justifying colonial rule.

**Activity.** Ask your grandparents or elders how their school was organised. Did they have a fixed timetable, exams, fees, uniforms? Did they learn in their home language? Make a three-column table: pathshala (1830s), their school, your school.

> **Did you know?** Pathshala teachers often taught arithmetic using mental methods so quick that British observers were astonished — skills that rote textbook learning sometimes lost.

story.title: Gopal's Two Schools — an imagined tale from a Bengal village, 1830s–1860s

parts.md: Gopal was nine when he began going to the pathshala under the big banyan near the village pond. Guru-mashai sat on a mat; about fifteen boys of all ages sat around him. Gopal's father, a peasant, paid a little rice and a few coins after the harvest; the grain-merchant's son paid more. Gopal wrote letters on palm leaves and in sand, recited multiplication tables in a sing-song and learned to calculate land measurements and grain prices in his head faster than the merchant's clerk.

When the paddy ripened, the banyan stood empty. Gopal and the other boys were in the fields with their fathers, cutting and carrying sheaves. Nobody scolded them. After the threshing, they drifted back to the guru, who simply picked up where each boy had left off. One winter a sahib with a notebook — people said his name was Adam — came and asked the guru many questions and counted the boys.

Years passed. Gopal grew up and became a farmer, and his son Haren joined the same pathshala. But by the 1860s things had changed. A government pandit came every few weeks with printed textbooks and a register. 'Classes will begin at a fixed hour. Fees must be paid monthly. An examination will be held at the end of the year.' The guru accepted the rules because the school would then receive a grant; the guru in the next village refused, and his pathshala slowly emptied.

That autumn the harvest came early. Haren had to go to the fields. When he returned after three weeks, his name had a red mark in the register. 'Irregular attendance — indiscipline,' the pandit wrote. Haren felt ashamed, though he had only done what his family needed. Several boys like him stopped coming.

Many years later, Haren's grandson read in a newspaper about a poet who had opened a school under the trees at Santiniketan, and about Gandhiji saying that working with one's hands was part of real education. The old man smiled. 'Under the banyan,' he said, 'we already knew that.' He was not entirely right — the old pathshala had its limits too, and few girls or children of the lowest castes sat there — but he understood that what counts as 'good schooling' depends on who makes the rules.

summary: The British saw 'civilising the natives' as part of their mission; education was a key tool.
William Jones (arrived 1783) and other Orientalists (Colebrooke, Halhed) respected ancient Indian and Persian learning.
Asiatic Society (1784), Calcutta Madrasa (1781) and Hindu College Benares (1791) came from Orientalist ideas.
Critics like James Mill and Macaulay called Eastern learning unscientific and pressed for useful Western knowledge.
Macaulay's Minute led to the English Education Act of 1835: English for higher education.
Wood's Despatch (1854) linked European education to trade, demand for British goods, morality and trustworthy civil servants.
Education departments were created; universities at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay were founded in 1857.
Missionaries (William Carey) set up the Serampore mission in 1800; after 1857 the government avoided supporting them directly.
William Adam found over one lakh pathshalas with 20 lakh children in Bengal and Bihar in the 1830s.
Pathshalas were flexible: oral teaching, fees by income, mixed groups, closure at harvest.
After 1854, government pandits (each for 4–5 schools), timetables, textbooks, fees and exams were imposed; grants went to schools that complied.
The new rules made attendance hard for poor peasant children.
Gandhi wanted education in Indian languages, hand-work and crafts, and self-respect; literacy alone was not education.
Tagore founded Santiniketan in 1901, blending creativity, nature, art and Western science; it grew into Visva-Bharati.

Money given by government for a purpose.

rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-national-move.title: The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947
rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-national-move.subtitle: From petitions in Bombay halls to the Salt March and midnight freedom — how Indians became a nation in struggle

sections.h: Who does this country belong to?
sections.md:
In 1857 the rebels had challenged Company rule, but they did not yet speak of 'India' as a nation of all its people. By the late nineteenth century a new question was being asked in newspapers, debating clubs and drawing rooms: **Who owns this country?** The answer that emerged was bold — India belongs to its people, of every class, colour, caste, creed, language and gender, and the British were taking its wealth and controlling its resources.

This chapter traces how that idea turned into a mass movement over about 75 years:

1. **Rise of nationalism** (1870s–1885) and the Indian National Congress.
2. **The Moderates and the Radicals** (1885–1915), Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi.
3. **Gandhi and mass nationalism** (1915–1922): Rowlatt Satyagraha, Khilafat, Non-Cooperation.
4. **Towards independence** (1922–1947): Salt March, Quit India, Partition and freedom.

> Keep track of *who* joined at each stage. The story is one of ever-widening participation.

In the 1870s and 1880s, a class of educated Indians — lawyers, teachers, journalists — began forming **political associations**. Most were in **Bombay, Calcutta and Madras**: the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha**, the **Indian Association**, the **Madras Mahajan Sabha**, the **Bombay Presidency Association**, and others. They worked for the idea of *sarvajanik* — 'of or for all the people'.

Several British actions angered them:
- The **Arms Act (1878)** disallowed Indians from possessing arms.
- The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** allowed the government to confiscate the assets of newspapers that published anything 'objectionable'.
- In **1883** the **Ilbert Bill**, which would have allowed Indian judges to try British or European persons, was furiously opposed by white people and forced to be withdrawn. This showed the racial attitudes of the British clearly.

**The Indian National Congress** was formed when **72 delegates** from across the country met at **Bombay in December 1885**. Early leaders included **Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji, W.C. Bonnerji, Surendranath Banerji and Romesh Chandra Dutt**. A retired British official, **A.O. Hume**, helped bring them together.

**A nation in the making.** In its first twenty years, the Congress was 'moderate' in objectives and methods. It demanded:
- a greater voice for Indians in government and administration;
- that the Legislative Councils be made more representative and given more power;
- Indians in high positions; civil service exams held in India as well as London;
- separation of the judiciary from the executive, repeal of the Arms Act, freedom of speech and expression.

On the economy, the Moderates argued British rule had led to poverty and famines: rising land revenue had impoverished peasants and zamindars; exports of grain caused food shortages. Naoroji's book *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* developed the idea of the **'drain of wealth'**. They demanded reduced revenue, cut military spending and more funds for irrigation, and they spoke out about Indian workers abroad.

Their methods: petitions, meetings, newspapers and speeches to educate public opinion, believing the British respected freedom and justice and would accept just demands.
keyTerms: Sarvajanik — of or for all the people
Drain of wealth — Naoroji's idea that British rule carried India's wealth to Britain
Moderates — early Congress leaders who used petitions and dialogue

check.q: Where and when did the Indian National Congress first meet?
check.why: Seventy-two delegates met at Bombay in December 1885 to form the Indian National Congress.

sections.h: Freedom is our birthright: the Radicals and Swadeshi
sections.md:
By the 1890s many Indians began to question the Moderates' politics. In Bengal, Maharashtra and Punjab, leaders like **Bipin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai** (remembered together as *Lal–Bal–Pal*) explored more radical objectives and methods. They criticised the Moderates for their 'politics of prayers', stressed self-reliance and constructive work, and argued that people must rely on their own strength, not the 'good' intentions of the government. Tilak raised the cry: **"Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!"**

**Partition of Bengal, 1905.** Viceroy **Curzon** partitioned Bengal — then the biggest province of British India, including Bihar and parts of Odisha. The British said it was for administrative convenience, but it was closely tied to the interests of British officials and to dividing Bengali politics; non-Bengali areas were not removed, and Muslim- and Hindu-majority regions were separated. It infuriated people all over India.

The **Swadeshi movement** followed. In Bengal it opposed partition and encouraged **swadeshi** (of one's own country) goods: Indian-made cloth, national education, and boycott of British goods. Some revolutionaries also argued for violence to overthrow the British.

**1906: the All India Muslim League** was formed at Dacca by a group of Muslim landlords and nawabs. It supported the partition of Bengal and demanded separate electorates for Muslims, which the government conceded in **1909**. Some seats in the councils were now reserved for Muslims, to be elected by Muslim voters. This tempted politicians to gather a following by distributing favours to their own religious groups.

**1907: the Congress split.** Moderates were opposed to boycott and the use of force. The two groups split at Surat, and came together again in **December 1915**. In **1916** the Congress and the Muslim League signed the historic **Lucknow Pact** and decided to work together for representative government in the country.

check.q: Why did the Partition of Bengal (1905) anger people?
options: It was seen as a way to divide Bengali politics and people
It moved the capital to Bombay
check.why: Though called an administrative step, the partition was widely seen as a move to divide and weaken Bengal's nationalist politics.

sections.md:
After 1919 the movement gradually became a **mass movement** — peasants, tribals, students and women joined in large numbers, sometimes factory workers too. Why?

**The First World War (1914–18)** changed the economic and political situation. Defence spending rose, financed by war loans and higher taxes on individual incomes and business profits. Prices rose sharply; ordinary people struggled. Business groups made huge profits from the war and demanded more opportunities. The army recruited soldiers from villages. Indian soldiers abroad saw how people elsewhere resisted imperial powers. The **Russian Revolution of 1917** inspired many.

**Enter Mahatma Gandhi.** Gandhi, aged 46, arrived in India from **South Africa in 1915**, where he had led movements against racist restrictions using **satyagraha** — non-violent struggle. He spent his first year travelling throughout India, understanding people. His early local movements were at **Champaran (1917)** for indigo farmers, **Kheda (1918)** for peasants, and **Ahmedabad (1918)** for mill workers.

**The Rowlatt Satyagraha.** In **1919** Gandhi called for a satyagraha against the **Rowlatt Act** that the British had just passed. It curbed fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and strengthened police powers. Gandhi, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and others felt the government had no right to restrict basic freedoms; they criticised the Act as 'devilish' and tyrannical. April 6, 1919 was observed as a day of non-violent opposition — 'humiliation and prayer' — with hartals.

**Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919).** In Amritsar, on **Baisakhi day**, General **Dyer** ordered troops to open fire on a peaceful gathering inside an enclosed garden. Hundreds were killed. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest.

fig.caption: The national movement at a glance.

check.q: What did the Rowlatt Act (1919) do?
options: Curbed fundamental rights and increased police powers
check.why: The Rowlatt Act restricted freedoms like expression and gave police wide powers, which is why Gandhi called a satyagraha against it.

sections.md:
The **Khilafat** agitation (1919–20) was led by **Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**. The Ottoman Sultan of Turkey, seen as the *Khalifa* (spiritual head of many Muslims), had been treated harshly after the First World War. Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause, seeing a chance to bring Hindus and Muslims together, and urged a combined campaign of **non-cooperation** for Khilafat and swaraj.

The **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920–22) gained momentum. Thousands of students left government schools and colleges. Many lawyers like **Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, C. Rajagopalachari and Asaf Ali** gave up their practice. Titles were surrendered; legislatures boycotted. People lit **public bonfires of foreign cloth**. The imports of foreign cloth fell drastically between 1920 and 1922.

People interpreted Gandhi's call in their own ways:
- In **Kheda**, Gujarat, Patidar peasants organised non-violent campaigns against the high land revenue demand.
- In coastal **Andhra** and interior **Tamil Nadu**, liquor shops were picketed.
- In the **Guntur** district of Andhra, tribals and poor peasants staged forest satyagrahas, sometimes sending their cattle into forests without paying grazing fees.
- In **Sind** (now Pakistan), Muslim traders and peasants were very enthusiastic about the Khilafat call. In **Bengal** too, the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance gave enormous communal unity.
- In **Punjab**, the **Akali agitation** of the Sikhs sought to remove corrupt mahants from gurdwaras.
- In **Assam**, tea garden labourers left plantations shouting 'Gandhi Maharaj ki Jai'.

People saw Gandhi as a kind of messiah who could help them overcome their misery and poverty.

**Chauri Chaura, February 1922.** A crowd of peasants set fire to a police station at Chauri Chaura (in present Uttar Pradesh); 22 policemen were killed. Gandhi called off the movement, as he felt it was turning violent and people needed proper training before mass struggles.

> **Did you know?** Gandhi believed means mattered as much as ends: a freedom won through violence, he felt, would carry violence into the free nation.

sections.h: Towards Purna Swaraj and the Salt March
sections.md:
After Non-Cooperation, some leaders, such as **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru**, formed the **Swaraj Party** within the Congress to argue for participation in councils. Younger leaders like **Subhas Chandra Bose** and **Jawaharlal Nehru** pressed for more radical action and complete independence. Meanwhile, Gandhi's followers did **constructive work** in villages: spinning khadi, removing untouchability, promoting education.

Revolutionary nationalists like **Bhagat Singh, Chandra Shekhar Azad and Sukhdev** were also active. In **1929**, Bhagat Singh and **Batukeshwar Dutt** threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly — not to kill but, as they said, to make the deaf hear. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed in **1931**. Bhagat Singh was 23.

**Simon Commission (1927).** A statutory commission headed by Lord Simon came to decide India's political future — without a single Indian member. It was greeted with the slogan **'Simon Go Back'**. During protests against it in Lahore, Lala Lajpat Rai was assaulted by police and later died.

**Purna Swaraj (1929).** At the **Lahore session** in December 1929, under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency, the Congress resolved to fight for **complete independence**. **26 January 1930** was celebrated as 'Independence Day' all over the country.

**The Salt March (Dandi March), 1930.** Gandhi announced he would lead a march to break the **salt law**, which gave the state a monopoly over the manufacture and sale of salt. Salt is needed by everyone — rich and poor — so taxing it was seen as sinful. Gandhi and his followers marched over **240 miles (about 385 km)** from **Sabarmati to the coastal town of Dandi**, where they broke the law by gathering natural salt on the seashore and boiling seawater to make salt. Peasants, tribals and women participated in large numbers. A business federation published a pamphlet on the salt issue. The government tried to crush the movement through brutal action against peaceful satyagrahis; thousands were sent to jail.

**Government of India Act 1935** prescribed provincial autonomy. In **1937**, elections were held to provincial legislatures; the Congress formed governments in 7 of 11 provinces.

sections.md:
**The Second World War** broke out in September **1939**. Critical of Hitler, Congress leaders were ready to support the British war effort — but in return wanted India granted independence after the war. The British refused. Congress ministries **resigned** in protest.

**Quit India (August 1942).** Gandhi decided to begin a new phase of struggle. The British must **quit India** immediately, he said, and he gave the call **'Do or Die'**. The British responded with severe repression; leaders were jailed at once. Yet the movement spread: people attacked symbols of British authority, governments were set up in some areas (parallel governments), and youth, peasants and women joined. By the end of 1943 over 90,000 people were arrested and around 1,000 killed in police firing. The British realised that ruling India was becoming impossible.

**Subhas Chandra Bose**, a radical nationalist with socialist leanings, did not share Gandhi's commitment to ahimsa. He was ousted from the Congress presidency (1939) and sought help from Japan, forming the **Indian National Army (INA)** to free India. The INA marched towards India in 1944 but the campaign failed. INA trials in 1945–46 stirred huge public sympathy.

**Growing communal politics.** From the late 1930s, the **Muslim League** began viewing Muslims as a separate 'nation' from Hindus. In **1940** it moved a resolution demanding 'Independent States' for Muslims in the north-western and eastern areas of the country. Its support grew during the war.

**Towards independence.** After the war, the British opened negotiations. The talks failed because the League saw itself as the sole spokesperson of India's Muslims. In **1946** the **Cabinet Mission** proposed a loose three-tier federation; it was not accepted by all. The League called for a **'Direct Action Day'** on **16 August 1946**, and riots broke out in Calcutta, spreading to other parts of north India. By March 1947, the Congress high command decided to agree to divide Punjab into two halves, and the same for Bengal.

On **15 August 1947**, India became independent, and **Pakistan** was created. Partition brought immense suffering: millions were uprooted, many lost their lives, and refugees crossed new borders in trains, carts and on foot. The joy of freedom was mixed with sorrow.

rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-women-caste-r.title: Women, Caste and Reform
rd-school-c8-social-a.hist-women-caste-r.subtitle: How brave reformers, books and new laws began to question customs that had seemed unchangeable

sections.md:
Picture a girl in 1800. In many communities she might be married before she turned ten. If her husband died, she might be pressured to die on his funeral pyre — a practice called **sati** — praised by some as the 'virtuous' choice. If she survived as a widow, she could not remarry. Most girls never learnt to read. Property rights for women were very limited.

Picture also a boy born into a so-called 'low' caste. He might not be allowed to enter temples, draw water from the village well, or study. Communities like the **'untouchables'** were treated as impure and kept out of everyday life.

Within a century, these customs were being openly questioned in newspapers, books, meetings and courtrooms. How did that happen? This chapter tells the story of **reformers**, the **new print culture**, **laws** and the struggles of women and lower castes themselves.

> Remember: change came slowly, unevenly and with fierce opposition. Many of these struggles are still unfinished.

sections.h: Working towards change: Rammohun Roy and sati
sections.md:
From the early nineteenth century, debates about social customs took a new form. **Books, newspapers, magazines, leaflets and pamphlets** were printed in large numbers, cheaper than manuscripts, and read by ordinary people — often in local languages. Debates reached wider audiences.

**Raja Rammohun Roy (1772–1833)** is one of the best-known reformers. He founded a reform association known as the **Brahmo Sabha** (later the **Brahmo Samaj**) in Calcutta. He wanted to spread Western education and bring about greater freedom and equality for women.

Rammohun was moved by the suffering of widows and began a campaign against **sati**. He was well-versed in Sanskrit, Persian and other languages, and tried to show through his writings that ancient texts did *not* sanction widow burning. This was a powerful strategy: reformers often argued that their ideas were rooted in the oldest sacred texts.

The British officials listened, and in **1829 sati was banned**.

> **Did you know?** Many reformers used the argument 'our ancient tradition was better than the present custom'. It let them call for change while answering critics who said reform was simply copying the West.

**Widow remarriage.** **Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar** (1820–91), a scholar and reformer in Bengal, used ancient texts to argue that widows could remarry. The British accepted his suggestion and a law permitting widow remarriage was passed in **1856**. Those who opposed it boycotted Vidyasagar.

In western India, **Veerasalingam Pantulu** formed an association for widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking areas of Madras Presidency. Swami **Dayanand Saraswati**, who founded the **Arya Samaj** in 1875, also supported widow remarriage. Still, the number of widows who actually remarried stayed low; society did not easily accept them.

**Girls begin going to school.** Many reformers felt education for girls was necessary to improve their lives. Vidyasagar and others in Bengal, and reformers in Bombay, set up schools for girls in the mid-nineteenth century. Many parents feared that schools would take girls away from home, stop them from doing domestic duties, and that travelling through public places would corrupt them. So in the nineteenth century, many educated women learnt at home from liberal fathers or husbands.

In the later part of the century, schools for girls were set up by the Arya Samaj in Punjab and by **Jyotirao Phule** in Maharashtra.

In aristocratic Muslim households in north India, women learnt to read the Koran in Arabic, taught by women who came home. Reformers like **Mumtaz Ali** reinterpreted verses from the Koran to argue for women's education. The **Begums of Bhopal** played a notable role in promoting education among women and started a primary school for girls at Aligarh. Another remarkable woman, **Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain**, started schools for Muslim girls in **Patna and Calcutta**. She was a fearless critic of conservative ideas.

sections.md:
From the early twentieth century, women themselves began writing, speaking and organising. Their voices carried a sharpness that male reformers often lacked.

- **Begum Rokeya** wrote a satire called *Sultana's Dream* (1905) imagining a place called Ladyland, where women had the freedom to study, work and create inventions — like controlling rain and travelling in air cars — while men were kept in seclusion. It turned the world upside down to make readers think.
- **Pandita Ramabai**, a great Sanskrit scholar, felt that Hinduism was oppressive towards women and wrote a book about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women. She founded a **widows' home at Poona** to provide shelter to widows treated badly by their husbands' relatives; women were trained there to support themselves economically.
- **Tarabai Shinde**, educated at home in Poona, published a book, *Stripurushtulna* (A Comparison between Women and Men), criticising the social differences between men and women.

Not everyone was happy. Many orthodox Hindus and Muslims worried that Indian women were adopting Western ways and that this would corrupt culture and break up homes. Some women even wrote and spoke against reform.

By the early twentieth century, women worked politically too: they formed associations and pushed for **female suffrage** (the right to vote) and better health care and education. Some joined nationalist and socialist movements.

**Laws on child marriage.** Nationalist leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose supported demands for greater equality for women. In **1929** the **Child Marriage Restraint Act** was passed without the fierce opposition earlier laws faced: it said no man below 18 and no woman below 16 could marry. (These limits were later raised to 21 and 18.)

sections.md:
Some reformers also criticised **caste inequalities**. Rammohun Roy translated an old Buddhist text critical of caste. The **Prarthana Samaj** (western India) adhered to the tradition of **bhakti**, which believed in spiritual equality of all castes. In Bombay, the **Paramhans Mandali** (1840) worked for the abolition of caste; many members were upper-caste and had to hold meetings secretly, sharing food cooked by lower-caste people to break caste rules.

**Missionaries** set up schools for tribal groups and 'lower'-caste children, helping some to gain new skills.

**New work, new hope.** In the nineteenth century, many poor people from lower castes left villages to work in growing cities — in factories, municipalities, as porters, diggers, sweepers or road builders. Some went to plantations in Assam, Mauritius, Trinidad and Indonesia. Work there was hard, but it offered a chance to escape the oppressive grip of upper-caste landowners. The **army** also offered jobs: many Mahars, who were considered 'untouchable', found work in the Mahar Regiment. **B.R. Ambedkar's** father taught at an army school.

**Demands for equality and justice.** From the second half of the nineteenth century, people from non-Brahman castes began organising movements against caste discrimination and demanding social equality and justice.

- The **Satnami movement** in Central India was founded by **Ghasidas**, who worked among leatherworkers and organised a movement to improve their social status.
- In eastern Bengal, **Haridas Thakur's Matua sect** worked among Chandala cultivators, questioning Brahmanical texts that supported caste.
- In present-day Kerala, **Shri Narayana Guru**, from the Ezhava caste, proclaimed the ideal of unity for his people: 'one caste, one religion, one god for humankind'.

All of them founded sects that criticised the caste system.

sections.md:
**Jyotirao Phule (1827–90)**, born into a low-caste family, studied in a Christian missionary school. He developed his own ideas about the injustices of caste society. He attacked the Brahmans' claim that they were superior because they were *Aryans*. Phule argued that the Aryans were outsiders who came from outside the subcontinent and defeated and subjugated the true children of the country — those who had lived there before them. He claimed that before Aryan rule there existed a golden age when warrior-peasants tilled the land and ruled justly.

Phule proposed that the **Shudras** (labouring castes) and **Ati Shudras** ('untouchables') should unite to challenge caste discrimination. The **Satyashodhak Samaj** (1873), founded by Phule, propagated caste equality.

In **1873**, Phule wrote a book named ***Gulamgiri*** (slavery). Some ten years earlier the American Civil War had ended slavery in America. Phule dedicated his book to all those Americans who had fought to free slaves, linking the conditions of 'lower' castes in India and Black slaves in America.

Phule's concern extended to women too. With his wife **Savitribai Phule**, he opened schools for girls. Savitribai is remembered as one of India's first women teachers.

**B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956)**, born into a Mahar family, experienced caste discrimination in school: he had to sit outside on the ground, and was not allowed to drink water from taps used by upper-caste children. After studying in the USA and England, he returned and wrote extensively against caste. In **1927** he started a **temple entry movement**, in which his Mahar followers participated. Brahman priests were outraged when Dalits used water from a temple tank. Ambedkar led three such movements between 1927 and 1935. His aim was to make everyone see the power of caste prejudices in society.

**E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)** came from a middle-class family. He had been an ascetic and studied Sanskrit scriptures. He became a Congress member but left in disgust when, at a feast organised by nationalists, seating arrangements followed caste distinctions — lower castes made to sit at a distance. Periyar founded the **Self Respect Movement**. He argued that untouchables were the true upholders of an original Tamil and Dravidian culture that had been subjugated by Brahmans. He was an outspoken critic of Hindu scriptures, especially the Codes of Manu, and of texts that he felt established Brahman authority and male control over women.

These assertions did not go unchallenged. Upper-caste nationalist leaders and orthodox groups responded by founding *Sanatan Dharma Sabhas* and the *Bharat Dharma Mahamandal*, arguing for respecting caste as a sacred institution.

check.why: Phule dedicated Gulamgiri (1873) to Americans who fought against slavery, linking caste oppression in India with slavery in America.

sections.md:
Reform also came through organisations rooted in religious traditions.

- **Brahmo Samaj** (1830): prohibited all forms of idolatry and sacrifice; believed in the Upanishads; forbade members from criticising other religious practices. It drew on Christianity's ideals too, particularly its messages of love and compassion.
- **Derozio and Young Bengal**: **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio**, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, in the 1820s, encouraged students to question all authority. His students, the 'Young Bengal Movement', attacked tradition, demanded education for women and campaigned for freedom of thought.
- **Ramakrishna Mission**: named after **Ramakrishna Paramhansa**, Swami Vivekananda's guru. The mission stressed the ideal of salvation through social service and selfless action.
- **Prarthana Samaj** (1867, Bombay): sought to remove caste restrictions, abolish child marriage, encourage women's education and end the ban on widow remarriage.
- **Veda Samaj** (1864, Madras): inspired by the Brahmo Samaj; worked to abolish caste distinctions and promote widow remarriage and women's education.
- **Aligarh Movement**: the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College**, founded by **Sayyid Ahmed Khan** in **1875** at Aligarh, later became the Aligarh Muslim University. It offered modern education, including Western science, to Muslims.
- **Singh Sabha Movement**: the first Singh Sabhas, reform organisations of the Sikhs, were formed at **Amritsar in 1873** and at **Lahore in 1879**. They sought to rid Sikhism of superstitions, caste distinctions and practices seen as non-Sikh; they promoted education among the Sikhs.

> **Did you know?** The word 'reform' meant different things to different groups. For some it meant returning to an imagined pure past; for others it meant boldly building something new. Both kinds shaped modern India.

summary: Print — books, newspapers, pamphlets — spread debates about social customs to many readers.

rd-school-c9-english-a.ch1-fun-they-had.title: The Fun They Had — Isaac Asimov
rd-school-c9-english-a.ch1-fun-they-had.subtitle: In 2157, a girl finds a paper book and discovers what school used to be

sections.md:
Imagine holding something so strange you can hardly name it: a pile of yellowed sheets, the words printed in one place, refusing to scroll. When you turn back a page, the same words are still sitting there, waiting. For eleven-year-old **Margie**, living in the year **2157**, this is a marvel — a *real book*.

That is the opening idea of **"The Fun They Had"**, a short science-fiction story by **Isaac Asimov**, first published in 1951 (in a newspaper's children's page) and later collected in his book *Earth Is Room Enough* (1957). It is the first chapter of the Class 9 textbook *Beehive*.

The story is tiny — barely a few pages — but it asks a question that feels sharper every year: **what is school actually for?** Is it only for pumping facts into heads efficiently, or is it also about friends, laughter, shared struggle and human teachers?

Asimov wrote this in 1951, long before personal computers, the internet, or online classes. Yet many readers who sat through lockdown-era video lessons in 2020–21 felt the story had been written about them.

> In this read: the author, the setting, a full scene-by-scene retelling, characters, themes, the irony at its heart, language work from the chapter, speaking and writing tasks, and model answers.

Asimov died in 1992, so his story is still under copyright. Read the original in your *Beehive* textbook (free PDF on ncert.nic.in); this companion explains it in its own words without reproducing it.

sections.md:
**Isaac Asimov (1920–1992)** was born in Russia and moved to the United States as a small child, growing up in Brooklyn, New York, where his family ran a sweet shop that also sold magazines — including the pulp science-fiction magazines he devoured. He became a professor of biochemistry at Boston University and one of the most prolific writers who ever lived, writing or editing **around 500 books**.

He is best known for:
- **I, Robot** (1950) and the **Three Laws of Robotics**, which shaped how people imagine robots and AI.
- The **Foundation** series, about a galactic empire's fall and a plan to shorten the dark age that follows.
- Hundreds of popular-science books explaining physics, chemistry, astronomy and history to ordinary readers.

Asimov believed deeply in **learning as joy**. He was largely self-taught in many subjects through libraries. It is no accident that a story by him is about a child who has every fact delivered by machine yet feels something is missing.

**Did you know?** Asimov disliked flying, so despite imagining interstellar travel, he travelled mostly by ship and train in real life.

sections.md:
Asimov builds his future with just a few touches, and each one matters:

- **Telebooks** — books are read on a screen. Margie's family has always had them; paper books are something her grandfather's grandfather remembered being told about.
- **Mechanical teachers** — each child has a robot-like teacher *in their own home*, with a large screen that shows lessons and asks questions.
- **A slot for homework** — children write answers in a **punch code** that they learned at age six, and push the sheets into a slot. The machine calculates marks instantly.
- **Fixed timings** — school happens every day at the same hour, except Saturday and Sunday. Margie's mother believes regular hours help little girls learn better.
- **Lessons adjusted to the child** — the machine is set to each child's ability, so each learns at his or her own pace.

Compare that with today. India already has smart classes, learning apps, AI tutors and auto-graded online tests. Asimov's 2157 is not so far away — which is exactly why the story still bites.
